weeks.title: Quick to Listen, Slow to Speak
weeks.theme: Listening is love’s first move: understand others first, and then you will be heard.
group: Read James 1:19-21. Why does “swift to hear” come before “slow to speak, and slow to anger”?
When was the last time you answered before you had finished listening? What were you rushing toward inside?
Whom will you truly listen to this week? Name the person, the time, and how you plan to listen?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a friend or an older person you haven’t been in touch with lately out for tea. Before you leave, pray: “Lord, today let me listen more and talk less.” At the table, put your phone away in your bag; ask questions and resist the urge to give advice. When you get home, write down one thing you heard from them, thank God for it, and pray for them by name.

lessons.title: Quick Listening Is Love’s First Step
lessons.hear:
When James wrote his letter, he was writing to believers scattered far and wide and facing trials. Under pressure, the easiest thing in the world is to start talking: to defend ourselves, to complain, to prove we are right. Yet right at that moment James says something that sounds ordinary but can transform every relationship: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

Notice the order of those three actions. Hearing comes first, and it is to be “swift”; speaking and anger come after, and both are to be “slow.” We usually do the exact opposite: we are quick to speak and slow to hear, and our temper outruns even our words. It is like a car with the gas pedal floored and the brakes gone. James reminds us, “the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). The “justice” I rush to announce often accomplishes nothing more than saving my own face.

Why is listening love’s first move? Because to listen is to move myself aside and make room for another person. If I am preparing my rebuttal while someone else is talking, I am really only listening to myself. True listening sets the “me” down for a while so the other person can be seen. This is exactly how God treats us: he hears our sighs and our prayers that we cannot even put into words. The psalmist loved the Lord precisely because the Lord had heard him (see Psalm 116:1). To be heard is, in itself, to be loved.

James goes on to say, “receive with humility the implanted word” (James 1:21). Only someone who knows how to listen to God will know how to listen to people. The one who often says before God, “Speak; for your servant hears,” will also learn to close his own mouth first in front of others. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your ears—and to open your heart as well.
lessons.light: Self-centered people talk in order to be heard; selfless people listen in order to understand. To be quick to listen is to let Jesus reign over my mouth—first handing the right to speak back to him, then making room for the other person. Relationships have an order: first with God, then with people. Only ears that often hear God can take in the heart of another.
think: In James 1:19-20, what does the order of the three “swift/slow” phrases tell us?
When others are talking, am I usually listening, or getting my own words ready?
Which conversation today can I deliberately listen more and speak less in?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you have always listened to me patiently; you even hear the sighs I cannot put into words. Forgive me for being so quick to speak and slow to hear, eager to defend myself without understanding others. Holy Spirit, open my ears and soften my heart, so that today I may be swift to hear and the people around me may feel your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, when talking with family or coworkers, pause for two seconds before you respond and restate what they said in one sentence: “So you’re saying … is that right?” Do this at least once.
lessons.quick: To be heard is to be loved; listening is love’s first move.
text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

lessons.title: Answering Before Hearing
lessons.hear:
A brother who works as a manager came home one evening. His daughter, in middle school, walked in and said, “Today someone in my class posted my business in the group chat …” Before she could finish, he said, “I told you a long time ago not to make friends with just anybody.” She froze, turned, went to her room, and shut the door. That night he waited in the living room for a long time, but the door never opened again. Only later did he learn that she had been shut out by her classmates that day and simply wanted someone to talk to.

Many of us carry an old mindset: people who talk well are the ones with influence; the moment someone opens their mouth, I need to hurry up with an answer so I look wise and helpful. In group chats especially, a message barely pops up before we are racing to reply, post a link, and draw a conclusion. God sees it completely differently: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). In God’s eyes, jumping in with an answer is not cleverness; it is folly.

Proverbs puts it even more bluntly: “A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion” (Proverbs 18:2). The root of our hurry to speak, it turns out, is often not love for the other person but love for ourselves: wanting to look knowledgeable, fearing being looked down on, needing to control the situation. This is self-centered socializing—the conversation becomes a stage and the other person an audience. The wise are different: “The ear of the wise seeks knowledge” (Proverbs 18:15). They treat their ears as vessels for learning, because they know every person carries things in their heart they do not yet understand.

So listening is not a waste of time; it is an investment of love. The next day that brother knocked on his daughter’s door and said, “Yesterday Dad spoke too fast. Would you be willing to tell me again? This time I’ll just listen.” In tears, she told him everything. He gave no lecture. He only said, “Thank you for telling me. Let’s figure this out together.” In that moment he was more of a father than ever.
lessons.light: Rushing to speak is often a small display of pride: leaving our proper place as a listener and grasping control. Humility returns to our proper place and admits, “I haven’t understood yet.” When I let Jesus reign, I don’t have to prove myself in every conversation; I can slow down in peace and let the other person finish first.
think: How do Proverbs 18:2 and 18:13 describe the person who rushes to speak?
At home or in group chats, on which topics am I most likely to answer before I hear?
Whom can I tell that last time I spoke too quickly, and ask them to tell me again?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often rush to answer because I want to look wise and stay in control. Shine your light on the “me” inside that loves to reveal its own opinion, and make me willing to slow down. Give me wise ears to understand the heart of everyone around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you once answered before you had heard them out (a family member, coworker, or friend in a group chat). Today, message them or tell them in person: “Last time I jumped to conclusions too quickly. Could I listen to you again?”
lessons.quick: Answering first isn’t clever; hearing someone out is wisdom.
text: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.
A man’s spirit will sustain him in sickness, but a crushed spirit, who can bear?
The heart of the discerning gets knowledge. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge.
A man’s gift makes room for him, and brings him before great men.
He who pleads his cause first seems right— until another comes and questions him.

lessons.title: A Time to Keep Silence
lessons.hear:
Ecclesiastes lists fourteen pairs of “a time,” and one pair is easy to skim past: “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Notice that silence comes before speech. This is not to say words don’t matter; it reminds us that words have their proper time—and often the most loving word is simply a stretch of quiet companionship.

How can we practice listening today? Here are three simple moves. First, put down your phone and turn toward the person. When someone starts talking, turn your screen face down and look them in the eye. That small gesture says, “You matter more than my notifications.” People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. Second, ask one more question and give one less answer. Instead of rushing to say, “You should …,” ask, “And then what happened?” or “What was going on in your heart at that moment?” Proverbs says, “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out” (Proverbs 20:5). A good question is like a bucket that slowly draws water up from a deep well. Third, receive the feelings first, then deal with the issue.

One sister’s coworker said to her in the break room, “I really can’t keep doing this.” She was about to say, “Just hang in there,” but she held back and said only, “It sounds like you’re really exhausted. Do you want to talk about it?” Her coworker talked for twenty minutes and finally said, “Thank you. I feel so much better.” She had not given a single piece of advice. She had only listened.

On the road to Emmaus, Jesus knew everything, yet he first asked the two discouraged disciples, “What things?” (Luke 24:19). He let them pour out all their disappointment, and only then did he explain the Scriptures to them. If even the Lord listened first, what are we in such a hurry for? Today, choose one person and lend them your ears.
lessons.light: Listening is a form of self-denial: setting aside my time, my attention, and the things I want to say—for someone else, not for myself. The “0” in 920 becomes very concrete here: when I am in no hurry to speak, the other person has room; when I rely on the Holy Spirit with my heart instead of hunting for answers with my head, I can hear the real need beneath their words.
think: Ecclesiastes 3:7 puts “silence” before “speak.” What does that remind me of?
When people pour out their troubles to me, do I rush to give advice, or can I receive their feelings first?
Whom will I lend my ears to today—and when and where?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the road to Emmaus you first asked your disciples, “What things?” and patiently heard out their disappointment. Teach me to listen like that: to put down my phone, turn toward the person in front of me, receive their heart first, and then speak a fitting word. Lead me today to the one who needs to be heard. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, arrange to have a drink or a fifteen-minute phone call with a friend or coworker who seems to have something on their mind. Put your phone face down, only ask questions without giving advice, and at the end thank them for sharing.
lessons.quick: Phone down, one more question, feelings first: lend someone your ears.
text: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

lessons.title: Job’s Friends: From Presence to Blame
lessons.hear:
Job’s three friends started out remarkably well. When they heard of Job’s disaster, they arranged to come together from far away. When they saw him, they did not recognize him, and they wept aloud. Then “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (Job 2:13). Those seven days of silence may be the most beautiful friendship in the whole book of Job.

The trouble began once they opened their mouths. As soon as Job voiced his pain, his three friends could not contain themselves: they began explaining, analyzing, and arguing, insisting that Job must have sinned to be suffering so. They said many things that sounded correct, yet they never understood the man in front of them. In anguish Job replied, “You are all miserable comforters!” (Job 16:2). In the end God himself spoke and told them, “you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7).

This holds up a mirror to us. Where are we most likely to stop listening? Often it is precisely when we feel most sure of ourselves. When a friend loses a job, a marriage hits trouble, or a child goes off the rails, we already have the answer in our heads, and we hurry to press it into their hands. The self-centeredness here is well hidden: I need to prove that I understand; I need things to have an explanation; I cannot bear a silence that has no conclusion. Selfless companionship, by contrast, can hold “I don’t know why either” and is willing to keep sitting on the ground.

God also shows the way to make things right at the end of Job: the three friends were to bring sacrifices to Job, and Job “prayed for his friends” (Job 42:10). They had to humbly admit they were wrong, and the wounded Job interceded for them. The relationship was restored through confession and intercession. Today, if you remember someone you once hurt with “all the right words,” now is a good time to turn back.
lessons.light: The failure of Job’s friends was answering suffering with their heads rather than accompanying it with their hearts. Use your head and you worry; use your heart and you find joy—and the same is true when we sit with someone who suffers. Pride needs an answer in order to stay in control; humility is willing to say, “I don’t understand, but I’m here.” That is returning to our proper place as human beings and leaving the explanations to God.
think: How do the “seven days and seven nights” of Job 2:13 differ from the long speeches that followed?
Have I ever used “correct reasoning” that only made a suffering person feel worse?
How will I make it right with that person: by confessing, by praying, or by being present again?
lessons.speak: Father, I am often like Job’s friends, rushing to give someone who suffers an explanation instead of truly staying beside them. Forgive the part of me that needs control and needs answers. Teach me to sit quietly with others and to keep trusting you when I don’t understand. And please heal those who have been stung by my words. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you remember a friend who was hurt when you “reasoned” with them, send them a message today: “Back then I said too much. Really, I just wanted to be with you.” Before bed, pray for them by name.
lessons.quick: Seven days of silence beat long speeches; presence comforts more than answers.
text: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.

lessons.title: Doers, Not Only Hearers
lessons.hear:
This week we began in James, and now we return to James. Right after saying “swift to hear,” James speaks of a different kind of hearing: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). Listening, it turns out, runs in two directions: toward people, we are to be swift to hear; toward God, we are to do what we hear.

James uses a mirror as an illustration. A man looks in the mirror, sees dirt on his face, then walks away and forgets it—so the mirror is no use to him at all. Hearing the word without doing it is just like that. We have read many truths about listening these past few days. If we go on interrupting people as before and replying in group chats before reading to the end, we have only looked in a mirror for a few days. Among the eight steps of changing a mindset, repetition matters a great deal: a new habit has to be practiced again and again before it moves from the head into life.

James also ties listening to the tongue: “If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless” (James 1:26). True religion, he says, is “to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). In other words, after hearing comes seeing, and after seeing comes drawing near. Ears that know how to listen will eventually lead to feet that know how to move.

Today, pass on what you have received. Perhaps you will teach your children at the dinner table to wait until others finish before they speak. Perhaps you will share in your small group a time when you “only listened and didn’t talk.” Perhaps you will walk alongside a new friend as they learn to listen to their own family. Multiplication isn’t about starting a class; it is letting others see in you a pair of ears the Holy Spirit has opened. Someone who has been truly listened to understands better how to listen to others—and so love spreads outward, ring by ring.
lessons.light: Hearing without doing is head knowledge; hearing and doing is a changed life. A changed mindset changes life, a changed life changes living, and changed living changes relationships. When I carry “swift to hear” into my family and small group, I am building God’s system: a community that listens to one another, so that God’s will is done on earth.
think: In James 1:22-27, how are “hearing” and “doing” related?
Over these past few days, when did I succeed at listening, and when did I stumble?
To whom will I pass on “swift to hear,” and in what way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for opening my ears these past few days. I don’t want to glance in the mirror and then forget. Help me practice day after day until listening becomes my very life. Use my ears and my feet to care for those in affliction, and let the people around me come to know your love because they have been heard. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, at family dinner or in your small group, share one experience of “hearing first, then speaking,” and invite a companion to keep practicing with you and remind each other.
lessons.quick: Do what you hear, and love travels from your ears to your feet.
text: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.
