weeks.title: Death and Life in the Tongue
weeks.theme: The tongue can build up or tear down; changing our words begins with changing our hearts.
group: Read James 3:3-12. What images does James use to describe the tongue, and which one strikes you most?
Have you ever been deeply wounded by a sentence—or rescued by one? What were the words?
Whom will you use your tongue to “heal” this week? What is one sentence you plan to say to them?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, at a family gathering or shared meal, deliberately say one specific word of thanks or affirmation to each person at the table—especially the one who usually gets criticized most. Before you go, pray: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips” (Psalm 141:3). When you get home, pray for each person and thank God for the chance to speak words of blessing.

lessons.title: A Small Tongue, Great Power
lessons.hear:
James is a pastor with a gift for word pictures. When he talks about the tongue, he pulls out one image after another: the bit in a horse’s mouth, the small rudder on a big ship, a tiny flame, every kind of wild animal, a spring, a fruit tree. Every picture points to the same truth: “the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things” (James 3:5).

Start with the bit and the rudder. A large horse, a great ship—each has its direction set by something small. Words are the same: one sentence can decide where a relationship goes. One “I’m sorry” can turn a couple back from a cold war; one “You always do this” can push someone even farther away. Then consider the fire. James says, “the tongue is a fire” (James 3:6). One sour remark in a group chat is like a match tossed into dry straw: in no time there are screenshots, forwards, and people taking sides, and years of friendship go up in smoke.

What grieves James most is the tongue’s double life: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God” (James 3:9). We sing hymns at church on Sunday and chew out a coworker on Monday; we post a Bible verse in the group chat in the morning and gossip behind someone’s back at night. James sighs, “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (James 3:10).

This is a sobering passage, because James admits that “nobody can tame the tongue” (James 3:8). He doesn’t say this to make us despair, but to help us see clearly: willpower alone cannot rein in the tongue; it takes God. Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). Since the tongue holds so much power, all the more must it be placed in the hands of a greater King. The spring must be changed first; only then will the water that flows from it be sweet.
lessons.light: The tongue is the smallest member of the body, yet it so often speaks up for “me” and fights to win for “me.” A self-centered tongue lights fires for its own sake; a selfless tongue lets Jesus steer. No one can tame the tongue, but those who let Jesus reign can hand him the bit every day—the first step in changing our words by changing our lives.
think: In James 3:3-12, what power of the tongue does each image—bit, rudder, and fire—illustrate?
In which settings do praise and criticism take turns coming out of my mouth?
In which group chat or setting today do I especially need to hand my tongue over to the Lord?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you know that though my tongue is small, it often starts fires and hurts people. I confess that I can’t control it; I praise you and then turn around and criticize others. Be Lord of my tongue and take the rudder of my words, so that what flows from my mouth is sweet water. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group chat or conversation, whenever you are about to say something with a barb in it, stop and say in your heart, “Lord, please take the rudder.” Then rewrite it as a neutral or encouraging word before you send it.
lessons.quick: The tongue is small but sets the course of relationships—give the rudder to Jesus.
text: Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?
Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water.

lessons.title: What Fills the Heart
lessons.hear:
A retired brother was famous in his family group chat for his “sense of humor.” When his nephew did poorly on an exam, he wrote, “No worries—you were never cut out for school anyway.” When his daughter-in-law posted a photo of a dish she had cooked, he replied, “Looks like ordering takeout would be safer.” Everyone sent laughing emojis, and he thought he was quite the wit. Then one day his daughter told him privately, “Dad, every time you make a joke, someone ends up hurting inside.” He bristled: “I’m just telling the truth. Can’t a guy make a joke?”

Many of us hold an old mindset: once words are out, that’s the end of it; I just have a “quick mouth,” and it has nothing to do with my heart. “My tongue is sharp, but my heart is soft.” God’s view is exactly the opposite. Jesus said, “out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). Words don’t slip out by accident; they are the heart’s outlet. Squeeze a sponge and out comes whatever it has soaked up: fill it with vinegar and you get something sour; fill it with honey and you get something sweet.

Jesus also said something very sobering: “every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). This isn’t meant to frighten us, but to make us take our words seriously. God created the world with words; we are made in his image, and the words of our mouths also carry the power to build or to destroy.

That brother went home and thought about it for a long time. He realized that underneath his jokes was a heart that needed attention and needed to look clever. He confessed this sin to the Lord in prayer, then wrote a message of apology to the whole group, saying to his nephew in particular, “Your uncle was wrong before. You have your own strengths.” The chat was silent for a long while. Then his nephew replied, “Thank you, Uncle.” One heart changed, and a whole family chat began to change too.
lessons.light: Changing our words can’t start with the mouth; it has to start with the heart. This is the order of the five-fold change: a changed mindset changes life, and a changed life changes living—and our words are the most common fruit of daily living. Everything we do flows from the heart; when the Holy Spirit fills my heart, the life of Christ will naturally flow from my mouth.
think: In Matthew 12:33-35, what do the tree and its fruit stand for?
When I dress up my words as “just joking” or “just being honest,” what is hiding underneath in my heart?
Whom do I need to apologize to for a joke—or offer a word of affirmation I owe them?
lessons.speak: Father, you search our hearts, and you know where the barbs in my mouth come from. Forgive me for so often using jokes and “honesty” to cover my pride and resentment. Cleanse my heart and fill it with your love, so that what comes out of my mouth heals and builds others up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a recent joke you made that embarrassed or hurt someone. Today, apologize to that person privately, and tell them one specific thing you appreciate about them.
lessons.quick: What fills the heart comes out of the mouth—change the heart, then the words.
text: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree corrupt and its fruit corrupt; for the tree is known by its fruit.
You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.
The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.
I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.
For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

lessons.title: The Tongue of the Wise Heals
lessons.hear:
One proverb sets the tongue’s two possibilities side by side: “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals” (Proverbs 12:18). The same tongue can be a sword or a medicine. Both a blade and a remedy enter the body; one leaves a wound, the other brings healing. Every time we open our mouths, we are choosing which one to pick up.

What does it mean to speak rashly? It means words that blurt out without passing through the heart or through prayer. Our emotions flare, and we hit send in the group chat; someone provokes us, and we dig up the thing that hurts them most. A sharp tongue is often very “accurate,” because we know exactly where the people closest to us are weak. But wounding someone with precision has never been the reason God gave us a tongue.

So how can our tongues become medicine? Today we can start with three small things. First, speak the truth, but with the intent to heal. “Truth’s lips will be established forever” (Proverbs 12:19). A doctor tells the truth in order to treat the illness, not to shame the patient. Second, give specific affirmation. “You’re great” is like candy; “Thank you for coming with me to the hospital last time—I really needed you that day” is medicine. Third, say a word that mends. A simple “I was too hasty that day” often stitches up a rift better than ten gifts.

A sister who teaches school had a child in her class who was constantly teased. One day she said in front of the whole class, “I’ve noticed he’s the best in our class at taking care of animals.” It was only one sentence, but from that day on the child’s eyes lit up. Today your tongue can be medicine for someone, too. You don’t need to say much—just say it truthfully, specifically, and at the right time.
lessons.light: A sharp tongue is a self-centered tongue: it speaks to vent, to win, to look superior. A healing tongue is a selfless tongue: it speaks so the other person can be made whole. Jesus is my example—what he said to the Samaritan woman and to Peter was the truth, yet every word carried restoration. A tongue under Jesus’ reign becomes a blessing to others.
think: In Proverbs 12:17-22, how are honest words and healing words related?
Which of my recent words was like a sword? Which was like medicine?
To whom will I speak a specific, truthful, healing word today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your words are the bread of life and a healing remedy. Make my tongue no longer a sword but a medicine that heals. Today, help me notice the person near me who is hurting or overlooked, and give me a fitting word so they may be comforted by your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to—or tell in person—someone who often gets overlooked (a coworker, a neighbor, a quieter member of a group chat), naming one specific thing they did well that you’re grateful for.
lessons.quick: The same tongue can be a sword or a medicine—choose to heal today.
text: He who is truthful testifies honestly, but a false witness lies.
There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.
Truth’s lips will be established forever, but a lying tongue is only momentary.
Deceit is in the heart of those who plot evil, but joy comes to the promoters of peace.
No mischief shall happen to the righteous, but the wicked shall be filled with evil.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

lessons.title: Peter’s Tongue Restored
lessons.hear:
Peter talked a lot, and he talked fast. When Jesus asked, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter was the first to answer. When Jesus said all the disciples would stumble, Peter instantly replied, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble” (Matthew 26:33). Peter’s tongue often ran ahead of his life.

Then came that cold night. In the high priest’s courtyard, a single remark from a servant girl was enough to make this disciple—who had just vowed to die with Jesus—say, “I don’t know what you are talking about” (Matthew 26:70). The second time, he denied it with an oath. The third time, “he began to curse and to swear, ‘I don’t know the man!’” (Matthew 26:74). In a single night, the same tongue went from promising to cursing. The rooster crowed, Peter remembered the Lord’s words, and “he went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75).

Peter’s failure is a mirror. Our tongues are most likely to run out of control at two moments. One is when we feel supremely confident and say too much. The other is when we are afraid and lie, shift blame, or deny in order to protect ourselves. The two look like opposites, but they share the same root: self. The first wants to look strong; the second wants to save face and stay safe.

But the story doesn’t end with weeping. By the Sea of Galilee, the risen Lord prepared breakfast and asked Peter three times, “do you love me?” (John 21:16). Three denials were answered with three restorations. Jesus didn’t silence Peter from then on; instead, at Pentecost, Peter was the first to stand up and preach. A tongue corrected by the Lord can be used by the Lord again. Today, if you regret words you have spoken, don’t stay stuck in self-blame. Bring them to the Lord, let him heal you, and let him send you out.
lessons.light: When Peter said too much, it was pride leaving its proper place; when he denied the Lord in fear, it was self-preservation. Both are the self-centered life. The way back is to return humbly to our proper place—admitting, “I’m not as strong as I thought”—and then letting Jesus reign. The Lord corrects not only our mouths but, even more, our hearts.
think: In Matthew 26:69-75, how do Peter’s words spiral out of control step by step?
Does my tongue lose control more often when I feel confident or when I feel afraid?
What words have I spoken that I need to bring to the Lord and make right with someone?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, like Peter I sometimes say too much, and other times lie or shift blame out of fear. Thank you for not throwing me away, but turning to look at me and restore me. Heal my tongue and renew my heart, so that my words match my life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, review what you said today and find one sentence where you “said too much” or spoke “to protect yourself.” If it involved someone else, take the initiative tomorrow to clarify or apologize.
lessons.quick: A tongue the Lord has corrected can be used by him again.
text: Now Peter was sitting outside in the court, and a maid came to him, saying, “You were also with Jesus, the Galilean!”
But he denied it before them all, saying, “I don’t know what you are talking about.”
When he had gone out onto the porch, someone else saw him and said to those who were there, “This man also was with Jesus of Nazareth.”
Again he denied it with an oath, “I don’t know the man.”
After a little while those who stood by came and said to Peter, “Surely you are also one of them, for your speech makes you known.”
Then he began to curse and to swear, “I don’t know the man!” Immediately the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered the word which Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Then he went out and wept bitterly.

lessons.title: Set a Watch Before My Mouth
lessons.hear:
These past few days we have seen the tongue’s power: it is like a rudder, a fire, a sword—and it can also be a medicine. We have also seen that a tongue problem is a heart problem, and a heart problem must ultimately be brought before God. So we end not with a technique but with a prayer: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips” (Psalm 141:3).

David placed these words within a prayer offered like the evening sacrifice (see Psalm 141:2). He knew he couldn’t control his mouth, so he asked God to be its gatekeeper. Just as a city gate has guards, every word must pass God’s inspection before it goes out. This isn’t meant to make us afraid to speak, but to let every word we say pass through the filter of love.

A prayer like this needs repeating. Speech habits are formed day by day, and they must be renewed day by day. One simple way is to review your words each night: Which of my words today built someone up? Which hurt someone? To whom will I speak a good word tomorrow? The app’s Word Watch uses these three questions to walk with you through a nightly examination. You don’t need a perfect score every day; what matters is coming back to the Lord daily and letting him gently correct you.

Then pass this prayer on. You could ask your children at bedtime, “Did we say anything hurtful today?” Or you could agree with a spiritual companion to remind each other this month to keep watch over your lips. Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit” (Proverbs 18:21). When a family or a small group begins keeping watch over their words together, they will enjoy the fruit of peace and joy together.
lessons.light: Keeping watch over our words is the daily practice of “review, adjustment, repetition,” and it is also where multiplication begins. Change starts with me and spreads to my family and small group. A community of people who let Jesus guard their lips is building God’s system on earth, so that God’s name is hallowed in our words.
think: In Psalm 141:3, what does David ask God to do for him?
How have my words improved these past few days? In which situations do I still often lose the watch?
Whom will I invite to practice guarding our lips together?
lessons.speak: LORD, set a watch before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. I want to bring the words I have spoken to you each day; forgive, correct, and renew me. And use me to pass this practice on to my family and companions, so that together our words may bear the fruit of life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, examine your words using the three Word Watch questions. Then invite a family member or small group companion to ask these three questions together every night this month.
lessons.quick: One prayer each night: Lord, set a watch before my mouth.
text: LORD, I have called on you. Come to me quickly! Listen to my voice when I call to you.
Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.
Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.
Don’t incline my heart to any evil thing, to practice deeds of wickedness with men who work iniquity. Don’t let me eat of their delicacies.

weeks.keyText: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

weeks.title: Words That Build Up
weeks.theme: Speech seasoned with salt—truthful, kind, and timely—gives grace to those who hear.
group: Read Ephesians 4:29. What marks “what is good for building others up”? Which do you most need to practice?
Are you more prone to “truth without love” or to “nice words without truth”? Can you give an example?
To whom will you write a card or message this week with a word that builds them up?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, write three handwritten cards or three thoughtful messages—to one older person, one peer, and one younger person—each naming a way you have seen God’s grace in their life. Before you start writing, ask the Holy Spirit to bring fitting words to mind. Once they’re sent, don’t look for a reply; simply pray for them and thank God for blessing you through them.

lessons.title: No Corrupt Speech
lessons.hear:
In the first three chapters of Ephesians, Paul unfolds the greatness of the gospel: in Christ, God chose us, saved us, and made people who were once enemies into one body. In chapter four, his pen turns to the most everyday thing of all—how we talk. The order matters: grace comes first, then practice; we become new people first, and then we speak a new language.

Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). “Corrupt” carries the sense of rotten, like fruit left out too long. Rotten speech isn’t only coarse language; it includes sarcasm, mockery, judgment, and gossip—the moment those words leave our lips, the air turns sour. “Building up,” by contrast, is a construction picture: laying brick upon brick until a house stands. Every word we speak is either tearing down a wall or building one.

This passage draws three lines around good words. First, they are truthful: “speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25). Good words are not false words; lying among members of one body is like nerves sending the wrong signals. Second, they fit “the need”: we look at the situation and the other person’s need, and say what is fitting. Third, they give grace: when we finish speaking, is the other person closer to God and stronger—or more discouraged?

Why does this matter so much? Paul goes on: “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). The Spirit lives in us and is listening to our words. And the passage ends with a picture of grace: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). We can speak good words because we first heard the best word God ever spoke to us: you are forgiven.
lessons.light: Grace first, then practice—this is the 321 order: when our mindset changes, our life can change. I can speak words that build others up not because I am well mannered, but because Christ has forgiven me and the Holy Spirit lives in me. Words spoken under Jesus’ reign lay bricks for God’s system, one sentence at a time.
think: In Ephesians 4:25-32, what kinds of speech are to be put away, and what attitudes are to be put on?
Lately, have my words been tearing down walls or building them?
In which relationship today can I lay one brick of good words?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for forgiving me in Christ and speaking the best word of all over me. Remove from my mouth all bitterness, slander, and corrupt speech, so that I don’t grieve the Holy Spirit. Help me today to speak what is good for building others up as the need may be, so that it gives grace to those who hear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, at home or at work, deliberately speak three “brick-laying” sentences: one of thanks, one of affirmation, and one of encouragement—to the same person or to three different people.
lessons.quick: Every word either tears down a wall or builds one.
text: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.
“Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
and don’t give place to the devil.
Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need.
Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Speaking Truth in Love
lessons.hear:
One sister liked to say, “I’m just a straight shooter. I say what I think; I don’t beat around the bush.” When someone in her small group shared about a painful breakup, she said, “Honestly, it’s partly your fault—you’re too clingy.” When a coworker got promoted, she said, “You just got lucky.” There may have been some truth in what she said, but every time she opened her mouth, the room went quiet. She felt wronged: “What—do you want me to lie?”

This is a common old mindset: honesty and gentleness are an either-or. Another old mindset runs the opposite way: to avoid offending anyone, we say only pleasant things and don’t warn a friend even when we see them heading down the wrong road. The first uses truth as a club; the second uses nice words as a pacifier. Neither is God’s heart.

Paul says, “speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Truth is the content, love is the manner, and growth is the goal. Truth without love is like an unsterilized scalpel: it cuts, but it brings infection. Love without truth is like giving painkillers without treating the disease: comfortable for a moment, but harmful for a lifetime. Speaking truth in love means holding both: saying what is true, and saying it out of love.

How can we tell the difference? Ask yourself three questions: Am I saying this for their good or for my own comfort? Is now the right time, or should I wait and say it privately? Have I prayed for them before I speak?

That sister was gently reminded by her small group, and she came to see that being “direct” was often just an excuse for not wanting to pay the price of love. She began practicing saying one genuine word of affirmation before speaking a hard truth. A few months later, the sister who had gone through the breakup came to her on her own: “I want to hear what you think, because I know you really care about me.” Only when truth is wrapped in love can it reach the heart.
lessons.light: “I’m just direct” is often a shield for the self-centered life—it protects me from having to change. “I don’t want to offend anyone” is self-centered too—it protects me from rejection. A selfless person sets both aside: speaking truth for the other person’s growth, and choosing gentleness for the sake of their heart. The goal is that we all grow up into Christ, the head.
think: In Ephesians 4:15-16, what is the goal of speaking truth?
Am I more likely to use truth as a club or nice words as a pacifier?
Is there a truth I should have said but never have? How can I say it in love?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are full of grace and truth. Forgive me for sometimes hurting people with my bluntness, and other times being too afraid of people to speak the truth. Teach me to speak truth in love: to say what is true, and to say it gently; not for my own comfort, but for the other person’s growth. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a friend to whom you need to speak a hard truth. Today, pray for them first, then set a time to talk privately. When you speak, begin with a sincere word of affirmation, and then gently share your concern.
lessons.quick: Truth is the content, love is the manner, growth is the goal.
text: that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error;
but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.

lessons.title: Speech Seasoned with Salt
lessons.hear:
At the end of Colossians, Paul talks about how to relate to people outside the church: “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:5-6).

Why salt? Salt does three things that describe good words well. First, salt gives food flavor. Good words aren’t bland pleasantries; they make people feel seen and cared for. Second, salt preserves. Good words hold back gossip, resentment, and snide remarks from spreading through a community. Third, salt must be used in the right amount. Too little and food is tasteless; too much and it’s bitter. Good words need the right measure too—not the more the better, but just right.

Paul says “how you ought to answer each one”—notice: each one. For a discouraged coworker, a classmate who has been left out, a lonely elderly person, a friend who doubts the faith, the amount of salt differs and so does the way we speak. That takes wisdom, and even more, it takes prayer. Just before this, Paul says, “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” (Colossians 4:2). People who pray find their words seasoned.

Let’s put it into practice today. Before you head out in the morning, pray for three people you will meet and ask the Lord for a fitting word for each. In group chats, when someone shares good news, don’t just tap a like; type a specific blessing. When someone vents, don’t pile on with complaints; offer a word of hope. You could also message a friend who doesn’t yet know the Lord: “I was thinking of you recently—how are you doing?” No need to force in a Bible verse; just let them taste a little salt. One sister who had recently moved to a new country said that when she first arrived, a neighbor told her, “If you ever need anything, just knock on my door”—and she remembered it for years. That was a word seasoned with salt.
lessons.light: Salt always dissolves into the food; it doesn’t stand out, yet it flavors the whole dish. That is what selfless speech is like: not showing off, but letting the other person taste the grace of Christ. When we speak from the heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, we will know how we ought to answer each one.
think: In Colossians 4:2-6, how are prayer and speech connected?
Are my words more often bland, too salty, or just right?
To which friend outside the church will I speak a word full of grace today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you said we are the salt of the earth. Season my speech with your grace, so that my words are measured, warm, and full of hope. Lead me today to speak a word to the people around me—especially friends who don’t yet know you—that lets them taste your grace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a short greeting to a friend or neighbor outside the church: “I was thinking of you recently—how are you doing?” If they reply, respond thoughtfully to what they share.
lessons.quick: Good words are like salt: flavorful, preserving, and well measured.
text: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds,
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.title: Moses’ Rash Words
lessons.hear:
Moses is described as exceedingly humble (see Numbers 12:3), yet he stumbled over his words one day. In the wilderness the Israelites had no water and began complaining again. God told Moses to “speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water” (Numbers 20:8). But after gathering the assembly, Moses said, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10). Then he raised his rod and struck the rock twice.

Water still gushed out; God did not let the people die of thirst because of Moses’ failure. But God said to Moses, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel” (Numbers 20:12). Looking back on this event, the psalmist says, “he spoke rashly with his lips” (Psalm 106:33). Years of faithfulness were marred by one angry sentence.

This passage shows us three marks of rash speech. First, it often comes when we are worn out. Moses had been complained against again and again, and his built-up frustration exploded in that moment. Second, it often puts “me” at the center: “Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” In that moment Moses stepped into God’s place. Third, the job seems to get done, but the relationship and the witness have already been damaged. We are no different: misunderstood in a group chat or talked back to at home, we blurt out, “You people always …” It feels good while we say it, but we regret it afterward.

Yet Moses’ story did not become a story of failure. Deuteronomy closes by saying, “Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (Deuteronomy 34:10). Failure is not the end; coming back to God is the turning point. The first step of adjustment is admitting that those words left our proper place. The second is explaining and apologizing to the person who was hurt. The third is coming to God earlier when we are weary, so frustration doesn’t pile up until it explodes.
lessons.light: In that moment Moses left his proper place as a man and spoke as if he himself were giving the water—this is exactly pride: grasping God’s power. Humility returns to its proper place and lets God be God. Relationships have an order: first with God, then with people. When our relationship with God runs dry, our words easily turn harsh.
think: In Numbers 20:8-12, how did Moses’ actions differ from God’s instructions?
In what kind of weariness or frustration am I most likely to speak rashly?
Next time, how will I come before God before the words leave my mouth?
lessons.speak: Father, like Moses I have spoken rashly when I was tired and frustrated, putting myself in your place. Forgive me, and heal those I have hurt. Bring me back to you before my heart overflows, so that my words treat you as holy. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if you feel tired or wronged, pray for one minute before replying to any message. And say to someone your rash words have hurt, “I was too hasty that day. I’m sorry.”
lessons.quick: One rash word can leave regret, but returning to God brings restoration.
text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

“Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you, and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water. You shall bring water to them out of the rock; so you shall give the congregation and their livestock drink.”
Moses took the rod from before the LORD, as he commanded him.
Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?”
Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.”

lessons.title: Pleasant Words Are a Honeycomb
lessons.hear:
Proverbs says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones” (Proverbs 16:24). Honey isn’t made in a day. Bees fly out again and again to gather nectar, bringing it back bit by bit until a whole honeycomb is filled. Good words are the same: not one moving speech, but sentence after sentence, day after day, slowly building up sweetness in a family or a community.

These past few days we have learned about words that build up: truthful, kind, and timely. Today’s question is: How do we make this a habit and pass it on? Proverbs gives us a key: “The heart of the wise instructs his mouth” (Proverbs 16:23). The source of good words is not verbal skill but a heart nourished by God’s word. So repeated practice isn’t only repeatedly saying good things; it is repeatedly returning to God’s word and letting our hearts be instructed first.

Multiplication also starts close to home. One father began a small tradition in his family: once a week at dinner, each person takes a turn telling someone else, “Here’s something good I see in you.” At first the kids found it awkward, but it became the moment the whole family looked forward to most. One small group leader took the lead in her group chat: whenever someone shared, she didn’t just post an emoji but replied with a specific word of encouragement. Little by little, the tone of the whole group changed.

Paul says, “Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do” (1 Thessalonians 5:11). “Even as you also do” describes a habit. Today you can be a bee gathering nectar, and you can invite others to gather with you. One good word is a drop of honey in one person’s heart; when a whole group speaks this way, it becomes a honeycomb, and weary people who walk in taste the sweetness of God.
lessons.light: Multiplication isn’t copying a technique; it is passing on life. When I am first instructed by God’s word and then bring good words into my family and small group, the “9” of 920—the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit—bears fruit in my speech: love, joy, peace, kindness … flowing out word by word, so that God’s system is built up in everyday life.
think: In Proverbs 16:21-24, how are a wise heart and pleasant words related?
In my home or small group, is the atmosphere of our speech sweet or bitter?
What kind of “good words” tradition could I start at home or in a group chat?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your words are sweeter than honey. Instruct my heart with your word every day, so that sweet and healing words flow from my mouth. Use me to build a culture of exhorting and building one another up in my family and small group, so that weary people may taste your grace among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today at dinner or in your small group chat, invite everyone to tell one other person, “Here’s something good I see in you”—and go first yourself.
lessons.quick: Pleasant words are like honey; drop by drop they make a sweet home.
text: The wise in heart shall be called prudent. Pleasantness of the lips promotes instruction.
Understanding is a fountain of life to one who has it, but the punishment of fools is their folly.
The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds learning to his lips.
Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

weeks.keyText: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

weeks.title: Not Conformed in a Digital World
weeks.theme: Algorithms shape my heart every day, so God’s word must renew my mind every day.
group: Read Romans 12:1-2. What might being “conformed to this world” look like in our digital lives?
When you open your phone, what kind of content most often pulls you along? How does it affect the way you see people?
Which stretch of scrolling time will you trade this week for being with a real person?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, set aside two or three hours, switch your phone to Do Not Disturb, and go with a prayerful heart to spend time with someone: go grocery shopping with your parents, take a walk with your kids, or visit an older person who lives alone. Before you set out, ask the Lord to help you truly see the person in front of you. When you get home, write down one small thing you noticed during that time and thank God for it.

lessons.title: Transformed by a Renewed Mind
lessons.hear:
In Romans, Paul spends eleven chapters on the mercies of God: how we are justified by faith, how we are set free from sin and death, how we become God’s children. Then in chapter twelve he says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1). All the practice that follows is built on that mercy. We don’t change in order to be loved; we are willing to change because we are already loved.

Paul continues, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). To be “conformed” carries the idea of being pressed into a mold, like dough pushed into a cookie cutter that comes out in a fixed shape. Today that mold has a new form: the algorithm on our phones. It watches where we linger, what we like, how long we watch, and then serves up more of the same. We think we are choosing what to watch, but often we are the ones being chosen. Over time, the way we see people, events, and ourselves is quietly pressed into a certain shape: quicker to anger, quicker to compare, less patient to hear a whole story through.

Paul’s remedy isn’t to throw everything away, but to have our minds renewed. This is an ongoing action, like washing every day and refocusing every day. The algorithm shapes us daily, so God’s word must renew us daily. Whoever speaks most into my heart is the one shaping me.

The purpose of renewal is “so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). A renewed person scrolls with discernment: Is this message true? Does this video make me love people more, or look down on them more? With this block of time, does God want me focused on a screen or on the people beside me? Paul also warns us “not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think” (Romans 12:3)—a word especially precious in a world where everyone is on display.
lessons.light: The algorithm is centered on “me” and feeds me what I want to see; the Holy Spirit is centered on Christ and leads me to see what God wants me to see. Not being conformed to the world means letting Jesus reign in our digital lives too. Shifting from a human perspective to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal—only a changed perspective can change a mindset.
think: In Romans 12:1-2, what kind of action is “conformed,” and what kind is “transformed”?
Lately, what shape has my phone been pressing me into?
How can I let God’s word speak to me more than the algorithm does today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your mercy reached me first. I confess that I am often shaped by the world on my phone and become impatient, competitive, and restless. Renew my mind every day, so that even in front of a screen I may discern your will, and turn my eyes back to the people around me who need love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, the first time you pick up your phone, read a passage of Scripture or pray for one minute before opening social media. Tonight, message a friend you often see online but haven’t really talked with in a long time.
lessons.quick: Algorithms shape me every day; God’s word must renew me every day.
text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.

lessons.title: You Become What You Think About
lessons.hear:
A young brother who works at a tech company lies down in bed every night and says, “Just five minutes.” Before he knows it, it’s two in the morning. He isn’t watching anything bad: some funny clips, a few news stories, friends’ vacation photos, influencers’ unboxing videos. But the next morning he always feels empty and a bit irritable, and when a coworker gets promoted, he feels an inexplicable sourness. He doesn’t understand: “I’m just unwinding—why does relaxing make me more tired?”

This is a very common old mindset: as long as the content isn’t sinful, it doesn’t matter what I watch; scrolling is just rest and won’t affect my heart. But God’s perspective is this: you become what you think about. The heart is like a field—whatever seed you sow, that is the crop that grows. Sow anxiety, comparison, mockery, and endless stimulation night after night, and it’s hard to grow peace.

Paul wrote from prison, yet he wrote some of the most peaceful words ever penned: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Then he gave a menu for the mind: “whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). This isn’t an escape from reality; it is a call to choose the food of our minds on purpose. These words can serve as a sieve for our scrolling: Is this true, or an unverified rumor? Is it honorable, or is it mocking and exploiting people? When I’m done, do I want to love people more—or am I more anxious and more inclined to complain?

That brother made a small change: he stopped taking his phone into the bedroom, read a psalm before sleep, and brought three people on his mind before God. A few weeks later he said, “I’m sleeping better, and the next day when I see my coworker, my first thought is to pray for him.” When his mind got different food, he slowly became a different person.
lessons.light: Whoever holds authority over my thoughts is the one reigning. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him rule my eyes and that time before bed. Everything we do flows from the heart; guarding our thoughts guards our relationships—only a heart filled with peace can bring peace to the people around us.
think: Of the good things listed in Philippians 4:8, which is most often crowded out by what’s on my phone?
What most often feeds my mind right before sleep and first thing when I wake up?
What small change can I make tonight to swap out the food of my mind?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you know how often I scroll late into the night until my heart feels empty. Forgive me for carelessly feeding my heart, and let your peace guard my heart and my thoughts. Teach me to choose to think about what is true, honorable, and lovely, so that my heart may rest in you and I can bring peace to those around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, charge your phone outside the bedroom. Before sleep, read a psalm instead and pray by name for three people you will see tomorrow; tomorrow morning, greet one of them.
lessons.quick: You become what you think about—change what feeds your mind.
text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.
Do the things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me, and the God of peace will be with you.

lessons.title: Teach Us to Count Our Days
lessons.hear:
In Psalm 90, Moses describes human life this way: “it passes quickly, and we fly away” (Psalm 90:10). Then he asks God for one thing: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12).

To count our days is to know that time is limited, so every stretch of it is precious. What phones do best is make us forget to count. They never end: one video follows another, the feed can never be finished, and the next post is always more enticing than this one. An hour slips through our fingers like sand, without a sound. We often say we have “no time” to be with our parents, visit friends, or reply to someone we haven’t talked to in ages. But if we count honestly, it often isn’t that we have no time—it’s that our time has drained into a screen.

A heart of wisdom doesn’t throw the phone away; it hands time back to God and asks, “Where do you want me to spend this block of time?” Here is how to practice it today. First, see your time: open your phone’s screen-time report—not to beat yourself up, but to be honest. Second, swap out one block: choose a time today when you would normally scroll, such as after lunch or on the commute home, and replace it with something for someone else—call an older relative, reply to a friend whose messages in the group chat often get “seen” but ignored, or write a few lines to a coworker going through a hard time. Third, when you are with people, let your phone rest quietly in your bag.

One mother sat down to eat with her child one day without taking out her phone. Her child suddenly said, “Mom, you seem happier today.” It wasn’t that she was happier; she was finally present. Love takes time, and time is the gift God gives everyone in equal measure: twenty-four hours a day—the question is to whom we give them.
lessons.light: Time is entrusted to us by God; it isn’t ours. Self-denial means offering the time that feels like mine for Jesus and for others. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things—including the things on our phones. Seen with eternal eyes, being with one person is worth more than scrolling through a hundred more posts.
think: In Psalm 90:10-12, how does Moses view the time of our lives?
The people I say I have “no time” for—what screen time is actually crowding them out?
Which stretch of scrolling time today will I trade for which person?
lessons.speak: Eternal God, teach me to count my days, that I may gain a heart of wisdom. I confess that much of my time slips quietly away into a screen while the people around me are waiting for me. Help me today to give one block of time back to you, to spend it being with, greeting, and caring for a real person. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a time when you would normally scroll (like after lunch or during your commute) and call an older relative or a friend you haven’t been in touch with for a while. Talk for at least ten minutes.
lessons.quick: It’s not that we have no time—it drains into a screen. Trade one block for one person.
text: The days of our years are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years; yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for it passes quickly, and we fly away.
Who knows the power of your anger, your wrath according to the fear that is due to you?
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

lessons.title: One Look from the Palace Roof
lessons.hear:
“At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out … David stayed at Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 11:1). That sentence works like foreshadowing. The king who should have been at the front stayed home; the heart that should have been alert settled into idleness. Then, “At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing” (2 Samuel 11:2). David’s fall didn’t begin with some momentous decision; it began with an idle evening and a casual glance. After seeing, he sent someone to inquire, then sent messengers to bring her—from seeing to wanting, from wanting to taking—and a man after God’s own heart committed a terrible sin.

This passage rings especially true in the digital age. Today’s “palace roof” is in the palm of our hand: alone late at night, with one swipe we can see anything, look up anyone, and message anyone. Temptation often appears on our screens by itself when we are idle, tired, or lonely. And it isn’t only lust: snooping into other people’s private lives, repeatedly checking an ex’s posts, hiding behind an anonymous account to say what we would never dare say otherwise—all of it travels the same road: the eyes see, the heart wants, and the fingers do.

As you examine yourself, ask honestly: At what times and in what state am I most likely to let my guard down? The way to adjust is often to set up protection before that window arrives: keep your phone out of the bedroom, set time limits, and ask a trustworthy spiritual companion to keep watch with you. If an online habit has gone on so long that you can’t break free, seeking professional counseling is also God’s grace.

And in the end, David’s story is a story of grace. When Nathan exposed his sin, David made no excuses. He said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13). Then he wrote, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). No matter how many times you have fallen in front of a screen, this road home is open.
lessons.light: Self-centered eyes ask only, “What do I want to see?” Selfless eyes ask, “What does the Lord want me to see?” When David fell, his focus shifted from God to his own desire; when he was restored, his focus came back before God. Keeping our focus on Jesus, not on ourselves, is the most fundamental power for guarding our eyes.
think: In 2 Samuel 11:1-4, what steps did David take from seeing to sinning?
At what times and in what state am I most likely to let my guard down in front of a screen?
What protection will I set up before that window? Whom can I ask to keep watch with me?
lessons.speak: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. You know that when I am idle, tired, or lonely, my eyes often wander. Thank you that the door of your forgiveness never closes. Guard my eyes, and give me a trustworthy companion to walk in the light with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, set up one protection for the time when you are most likely to let your guard down (such as keeping your phone out of the bedroom or setting a time limit). Tell a spiritual companion of the same sex and ask them to pray for you and check in with you this month.
lessons.quick: A fall often starts with one idle glance; restoration starts with “I have sinned against the LORD.”
text: At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem.
At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.
David sent and inquired after the woman. One said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?”
David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in to him, and he lay with her (for she was purified from her uncleanness); and she returned to her house.
The woman conceived; and she sent and told David, and said, “I am with child.”

lessons.title: Within My House, Before My Eyes
lessons.hear:
When David was king, he wrote a psalm that reads like a policy statement: “I will walk within my house with a blameless heart. I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:2-3). Interestingly, the first battlefield in this king’s declaration isn’t the royal court but “my house,” and the first line of defense isn’t an army but “my eyes.”

These past few days we have learned that algorithms shape us, our minds need good food, our days must be counted, and our eyes must be guarded. Today we bring all this home and pass it on. A family can make a “family digital covenant” together. It needn’t be complicated—three or four points will do. For example: no phones at the dinner table; after a certain hour at night, everyone’s phone charges together in the living room; no forwarding unverified messages; never saying online what we wouldn’t say face to face. The point isn’t rules; it is a family declaring together: we want God to reign in this home, not the screen.

If parents want their children to keep these, they must keep them first. One father said his biggest turning point came when his child said to him one day, “Dad, you look at your phone during dinner too.” He didn’t get angry. He said, “You’re right. Let’s change together.” In that moment he taught his child not just rules about phones, but humility and how to admit when you are wrong.

Those without children can make the same kind of agreement with roommates, a small group, or a spiritual companion: reminding each other and keeping watch over each other. David said he would set no vile thing before his eyes; together we can say that we will set what is true, honorable, and lovely before our eyes—and set one another before our eyes as well. Not being conformed to this world isn’t a lonely struggle; it is a community being renewed together.
lessons.light: Change begins with me and then spreads to my family—this is the path of change from the inside out. Multiplication isn’t just passing on knowledge; it is living it out together. A home where Jesus reigns is a small expression of God’s system in the digital age, where God’s will is done in my house as it is in heaven.
think: In Psalm 101:2-3, which two places does David treat as his first battlefields?
In my home or living space, at which moments do screens steal us away from each other?
With whom will I make two or three digital agreements, and what will they be?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, reign over my home. I want to walk within my house with a blameless heart and set no vile thing before my eyes. Help me lead by example, and give me a humble heart, so that with my family and companions we may be renewed together in the digital world, keeping watch over one another and loving one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, with your family, roommates, or a spiritual companion, agree on two or three digital commitments (for example, no phones at the dinner table). Write them down, post them somewhere visible, and pray over them together.
lessons.quick: Not conforming to the world starts within my house and before my eyes.
text: I will sing of loving kindness and justice. To you, LORD, I will sing praises.
I will be careful to live a blameless life. When will you come to me? I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.
I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.
A perverse heart will be far from me. I will have nothing to do with evil.

weeks.keyText: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

weeks.title: Comparison and Social Media
weeks.theme: When I examine myself before God, I no longer have to live inside other people’s feeds.
group: Read Galatians 6:3-5. How is Paul’s “examine his own work” different from comparing ourselves with others?
What kind of posts most easily throw you off balance inside? What are you really longing for underneath?
Whose good news will you sincerely bless this week, and how do you plan to express it?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, write a gratitude list: ten graces God has given you this week, without comparing yourself to anyone. Then pick a friend you have secretly envied, and with prayer invite them for a meal or a phone call. Ask sincerely how they are doing, and listen for the struggles behind their posts. When you get home, pray for their needs and thank God for your friendship.

lessons.title: Let Each Examine His Own Work
lessons.hear:
The most common mental habit on social media is comparison. We scroll past a friend’s vacation photos and think about how we can’t get time off. We see a classmate promoted and feel like we are treading water. Someone else’s child wins an award while ours is still retaking a test. No one forces us to compare, but those neat rows of posts act like a wall of mirrors, constantly asking, “What about you? Are you doing better than they are?”

Paul saw this problem two thousand years ago. He wrote, “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else” (Galatians 6:3-4). Paul isn’t telling us never to evaluate ourselves; he is handing us a different measuring stick. Instead of measuring ourselves against others, we examine ourselves before God. Comparing eyes look left and right; examining eyes look up and look within.

Why does comparison hurt so much? Because it traps us in two errors: if we are better than others, we become proud; if we are worse, we feel inferior or envious. And we usually compare our backstage with everyone else’s highlight reel—our most honest struggles against their carefully curated best moments. That contest is rigged from the start.

Paul goes on, “For each man will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5). Just before that he said, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). The two don’t contradict each other: each person has a unique portion entrusted by God and doesn’t need to be like anyone else; at the same time, we are called to help carry the burdens others can’t bear alone. People who compare see only others’ crowns; people who love see others’ burdens. When I stop busily measuring whether I stand higher or lower than someone else, my hands are free to help someone up.
lessons.light: Comparison is a self-centered way of seeing: everything revolves around “How do I measure up to them?” Examining ourselves means returning to our proper place—honestly facing our own portion before God. Our focus is on Jesus, not on others. When God determines my worth, other people’s posts can no longer define me, and I am free to love them.
think: In Galatians 6:2-5, what does “bear one another’s burdens” mean, and what does “bear his own burden” mean?
Which part of my life do I most often compare with which part of someone else’s?
Whose burden can I help carry today instead of comparing?
lessons.speak: Father, you know how often I live inside other people’s feeds; comparison makes me proud one moment and insecure the next. Help me examine myself before you and accept the unique portion you have given me. Open my eyes to see not only other people’s crowns but also their burdens. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, whenever you catch yourself comparing while scrolling, stop and pray one sentence for that friend. Then choose someone who has been having a hard time and send them a private message: “Is there anything I can do to help?”
lessons.quick: Don’t measure yourself by others; examine yourself before God.
text: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.

lessons.title: My Worth Isn’t My Like Count
lessons.hear:
A young sister who had just started her first job couldn’t stop checking every few minutes after posting: How many likes? Who saw it but didn’t like it? If she got fewer likes than last time, she was down all evening. If a certain friend didn’t respond, she started wondering, “Does she not like me anymore?” She said, “I know it’s childish, but I just can’t help it.”

Behind this lies an old mindset: other people’s reactions determine my worth; I matter only when I’m seen and liked. Social media turns this longing into numbers, letting us measure how liked we are every day—even every minute.

Paul was compared to others too. Some in the Corinthian church promoted themselves and belittled Paul, saying his bodily presence was weak and his speech despised (see 2 Corinthians 10:10). Paul refused to compete with them. Instead he said, “they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:12). He was content to work within the limits God had assigned him. Then he wrote a sentence worth setting as your phone’s wallpaper: “For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends” (2 Corinthians 10:18).

This is God’s perspective: your worth isn’t found in your like count but in the price Christ paid for you. You are accepted not because your posts look good, but because God has already accepted you in Christ. When this truth sinks into our hearts, the like count goes from being a verdict to being just a number again.

That sister eventually took up a practice: after posting, she would put her phone down for an hour, and during that time she would intentionally respond to three friends’ posts—not with a like, but with a sincere sentence. She found that as she began caring about others, she cared less about whether she was being cared for. She laughed and said, “It turns out the best cure for like-anxiety is loving other people.”
lessons.light: Longing for affirmation isn’t a sin, but when we put it in God’s place, it becomes an idol. Letting Jesus reign means letting his acceptance be my final verdict. Let him who boasts boast in the Lord—when all the glory goes to God, I no longer have to fight for everyone’s attention.
think: In 2 Corinthians 10:12 and 18, how does Paul view commending ourselves versus being commended by the Lord?
When have likes or responses affected my mood and sense of worth?
How can I shift my attention today from “being seen” to “seeing others”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that before I had accomplished anything, you already loved and accepted me. Forgive me for so often measuring my worth by likes and responses. Let me rest in your commendation, and turn my attention to the people around me who need to be seen. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, leave a specific, sincere comment—not just a like—on three friends’ posts. Make sure at least one of them is someone who rarely gets responses.
lessons.quick: The one approved isn’t the one with the most likes, but the one the Lord commends.
text: For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.
But we will not boast beyond proper limits, but within the boundaries with which God appointed to us, which reach even to you.
For we don’t stretch ourselves too much, as though we didn’t reach to you. For we came even as far as to you with the Good News of Christ,
not boasting beyond proper limits in other men’s labors, but having hope that as your faith grows, we will be abundantly enlarged by you in our sphere of influence,
so as to preach the Good News even to the parts beyond you, not to boast in what someone else has already done.
But “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”
For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends.

lessons.title: Bless Others’ Good News
lessons.hear:
The Teacher looked at life and said something stinging but true: “Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes 4:4). Much of human effort is driven by comparison: I have to do better than my neighbor; I can’t lose to him. The result is a lifetime of toil that grasps nothing but wind.

Social media has made our “neighbors” countless. We used to compare ourselves with the people on our street; now we compare ourselves with the whole world. The Teacher offers a simple prescription: “Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind” (Ecclesiastes 4:6). One contented handful with peace beats two full fists and a restless heart.

The best antidote to envy isn’t pretending we don’t care—it’s blessing. Here is how to practice it today. First, admit it: when a post makes you feel sour inside, tell God honestly, “Lord, I’m envious.” Bring it into the light, and it can’t grow in the dark. Second, give thanks: count the “handful” God has given you—health, family, today’s meal, a friend. Gratitude turns our eyes from other people’s hands back to God’s hand. Third, bless: speak a sincere blessing to that person—not a token comment, but a private message: “I saw you got promoted. I’m truly happy for you; you’ve always worked so hard.” The first time may be hard, but when you speak a blessing by faith, the Holy Spirit often works in your heart, slowly turning the sour into sweet.

One brother secretly envied a classmate who had built a successful business, and it went on for years. One day he finally invited his classmate to dinner and said, “Congratulations. I’ve always admired you.” His classmate was silent for a moment, then said, “Honestly, these past few years have been really lonely. Thank you for still remembering me.” After that dinner, they became true friends.
lessons.light: Envy is self-centered: someone else’s good seems to rob me of mine. Selfless love can rejoice with those who rejoice (see Romans 12:15), because my blessing is in God’s hands, and someone else’s blessing doesn’t diminish mine. Blessing others is one of the most practical ways to let Jesus reign in my heart.
think: In Ecclesiastes 4:4-6, how does the Teacher compare “a handful” with “two handfuls”?
Which recent post made me feel sour inside? Am I willing to admit it honestly to God?
To whom will I speak a sincere blessing today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I get envious; when I see good things in others’ lives, I feel sour inside. Thank you that the handful of grace you have given me is enough. Give me quietness, and give me courage to speak a sincere blessing to the very person I envy, so that your love may turn the sour in my heart to sweet. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a post that made you feel sour inside. First pray for that person, then send them a private message with a specific, sincere word of congratulations or appreciation.
lessons.quick: The best antidote to envy is blessing the person you envy.
text: Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself.
Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.
Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.

There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.

lessons.title: When Asaph’s Feet Nearly Slipped
lessons.hear:
Asaph, the author of Psalm 73, led worship in the temple. Yet he admits honestly, “But as for me, my feet were almost gone. My steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:2-3). A worship leader nearly lost his footing in faith—because of comparison.

He saw people who didn’t fear God “always at ease, they increase in riches” (Psalm 73:12). Then he looked at himself, and the more he thought about it, the more wronged he felt: “Surely I have cleansed my heart in vain” (Psalm 73:13). We know this feeling well: I follow the rules and serve faithfully, while that person cuts corners and lives a glamorous life online. The poison of comparison eventually makes us doubt God’s fairness.

Asaph shows us how to review ourselves. First, he is honest; he doesn’t pretend to be more spiritual than he is. Second, he is careful: “If I had said, ‘I will speak thus’, behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children” (Psalm 73:15). He didn’t spread his bitterness around or post a snarky rant. Third, he found the turning point: “until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end” (Psalm 73:17). Comparison makes us see things with earthly, temporary eyes; God’s sanctuary gives us heavenly, eternal eyes. On a screen we see only a fragment of someone’s life; before God we see the whole story.

We can examine ourselves like this: Have I recently resented God because of comparison? Have I, out of envy, posted something snide online or been cold toward someone? If so, do as Asaph did: don’t rush to vent; bring it into God’s presence. At the end of the psalm, Asaph says, “Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). When God becomes my portion, other people’s blessings no longer threaten me.
lessons.light: Comparison looks at life with earthly, temporary eyes. When Asaph entered the sanctuary, he shifted from a human perspective to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. A changed perspective changes our mindset; when God is my portion, I move from resentment back to worship and contentment.
think: In Psalm 73:12-17, at which verse does Asaph’s heart begin to turn?
Has comparison made me resent God, or be cold or snide toward someone?
How will I bring this resentment into God’s presence and make things right with that person?
lessons.speak: Father, like Asaph, I have resented others’ success, and my feet have nearly slipped. Thank you for not giving up on me. Bring me into your presence and let me see life with eternal eyes. Be my portion, so that I am no longer ruled by comparison and am free to love others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If envy has ever made you cold or snide toward someone, reach out to them with kindness today: a greeting, a sincere compliment, or a practical act of help.
lessons.quick: Entering God’s sanctuary steadies our feet against comparison.
text: Behold, these are the wicked. Being always at ease, they increase in riches.
Surely I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocence,
For all day long I have been plagued, and punished every morning.
If I had said, “I will speak thus”, behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children.
When I tried to understand this, it was too painful for me—
until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end.

lessons.title: What Is That to You? Follow Me
lessons.hear:
After Peter was restored by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus told him how he would one day glorify God, and then said, “Follow me” (John 21:19). Peter turned around, saw John following too, and asked, “Lord, what about this man?” (John 21:21). Peter had just been restored, and his very first thought was a comparison: I have to walk this road—what about him?

Jesus’ answer was gentle and direct: “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me” (John 21:22). These words are the best medicine for a comparing heart. Other people’s paths, gifts, achievements, and sufferings are all in the Lord’s hands; your path is the one he wants you to walk with your whole heart.

These past few days we have seen that comparison makes us deceive ourselves, measure ourselves by likes, envy others, and resent God. There is only ever one way out: turning our eyes from the people to our left and right back to the Lord ahead of us. This takes repeated practice, because social media invites us every day to turn around and look at others. Each time you notice yourself comparing, gently tell yourself, “What is that to me? I will follow the Lord.”

Then pass this freedom on. Many people around you are being crushed by comparison: the college student scrolling through classmates’ glossy posts, the newly retired elder who feels useless, the new friend in the small group who always feels not spiritual enough. You can be the one who tells them, “You don’t have to live inside other people’s feeds”—not only with words, but by modeling it with your life: not comparing, not showing off, being genuinely glad for others, and walking peacefully on the road the Lord has given you. When a whole community is wholeheartedly following the Lord, comparison loses its stage and there is room to help one another grow.
lessons.light: “What is that to you? You follow me.” These words turn our focus from others back to Jesus. Our focus is on Jesus—not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. The 235 relationships among spiritual companions need exactly this freedom: not comparing ourselves with one another, but following the Lord together and helping one another grow.
think: In John 21:20-22, why did Peter ask Jesus what would happen to John?
What breakthroughs have I had with comparison these past few days? Where do I still often look back at others?
Who around me is being crushed by comparison? How can I walk alongside them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, like Peter, I am often barely restored by you before I turn around to look at others again. Thank you for gently calling me to follow you wholeheartedly. Help me walk peacefully on the road you have given me, and use me to walk alongside those who are crushed by comparison, so that they may find freedom in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a friend who often compares themselves with others or has been discouraged lately. Name one unique gift you see in them, and encourage them to walk their own road in peace.
lessons.quick: What is that to me? I will follow the Lord wholeheartedly.
text: Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Then Peter, turning around, saw a disciple following. This was the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ chest at the supper and asked, “Lord, who is going to betray you?”
Peter, seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”
