weeks.title: Online Words and Digital Sabbath
weeks.theme: Every word we post is a witness; a digital Sabbath brings our hearts back to God and to the real people beside us.
group: Read Ephesians 5:15-19. How are “redeeming the time” and “speaking to one another” connected?
Is the way you talk online the same as the way you talk face to face? Where is it different?
What digital Sabbath will you set aside this week, and whom will you spend that time with?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, set aside half a day for a digital Sabbath: let family and friends know ahead of time, turn off notifications, and put your phone in a drawer. Use the time to read a passage of Scripture, take a prayer walk, and then be with a real person—share a phone-free meal with your family or visit an older person. When it’s over, write down three things you are thankful for before you turn your phone back on.

lessons.title: Redeem the Time, Be Filled with the Spirit
lessons.hear:
Paul says we are to be “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). To redeem is to buy back, like going to the market and buying back something that had been sold off cheap. Time is a treasure God has given us, yet it so often gets sold off cheap: to endless scrolling, to one online argument after another, to content that leaves us emptier the more we watch. Redeeming the time means buying it back from these places and returning it to God and to people.

Paul goes on: “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). The contrast is striking. A drunk person is controlled by something from outside: their words lose all restraint and their actions spin out of control. Today there is a new kind of drunkenness: we open our phones and can’t stop; our emotions are dragged along by headlines; late at night we get more and more worked up in the comments, and wake up the next morning regretting what we said. Paul says Christians are to be filled by Someone else—governed by the Holy Spirit.

People filled with the Spirit speak differently: “speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father” (Ephesians 5:19-20). The first evidence of being filled with the Spirit, it turns out, shows up in our words: speaking to one another, praising, giving thanks. In the digital world this can be very concrete: sharing an encouraging song in a group chat, giving thanks for someone’s good news, saying “Thank you, Lord” in the middle of a chorus of complaints.

Finally Paul says, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). The internet often pushes us to win: to be the loudest, get the most shares, have the sharpest comeback. Christians choose another way: because we fear Christ, we don’t need to win; because we submit to one another, we are willing to take a step back. Let every word we post be a witness, and let our hearts regularly step away from the screen and return to God and to the real people beside us.
lessons.light: Being controlled by our phones lets “things” reign; being filled with the Spirit lets Jesus reign. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head—especially online. When our focus is on Jesus, our words turn from arguing to thanksgiving, and our time goes from being sold off cheap to being redeemed.
think: In Ephesians 5:15-21, what does the speech of a Spirit-filled person look like?
Online, what do I most often sell my time off to?
In which group chat today can I speak a word of thanks or encouragement?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, fill me with your Holy Spirit, so that I am not controlled by my phone or my emotions. Teach me to redeem the time, buying it back from empty scrolling. May every word I post online carry thanksgiving and the fear of Christ, and be a beautiful witness to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group chat you often take part in, share something you are thankful for, or reply to someone’s post with a specific word of encouragement.
lessons.quick: Redeem your time and let the Spirit govern your fingers and your words.
text: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father;
subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

lessons.title: Don’t Grab the Dog’s Ears
lessons.hear:
A brother in sales was courteous to everyone during the day, but at night he often argued with strangers in the comment sections of news sites. When he saw a comment he disagreed with, he couldn’t help replying; when the other person shot back harder, he wrote even more. One night he argued until three in the morning, lay in bed with his heart still racing, and spent the next day’s meeting in a fog. He told himself, “I’m just defending the truth.” But deep down he knew he really wanted to win.

This is an old mindset: people online aren’t really real, and words online don’t really count; when you see something wrong, you have to correct it, and if you don’t win the argument, you have backed down. Proverbs paints a vivid picture: “Like one who grabs a dog’s ears is one who passes by and meddles in a quarrel not his own” (Proverbs 26:17). Grab a strange dog by the ears, and you’ll get bitten if you let go—and bitten if you don’t. Many online flame wars are just like that: we were only passing by, but we grabbed hold, and in the end everyone gets hurt.

Proverbs also says, “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” (Proverbs 26:20). Every reply is another log on the fire. Sometimes the wisest response is no response—not because right and wrong don’t matter, but because this fire will only grow, and no one will come to know the truth any better through it. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

God’s perspective is that every person on the other side of the screen is made in God’s image, someone for whom Christ gave his life. This doesn’t mean Christians must always stay silent online. Sometimes we need to speak, but first we should ask: Am I speaking for the sake of the truth and the other person’s good, or to win? Could I write this in the tone I would use face to face? Am I willing to have a private conversation rather than shaming someone in public? That brother eventually set a rule for himself: no responding to any controversy online after ten at night. He found that when he looked again the next morning, most comments didn’t need a reply at all.
lessons.light: The root of online fighting is often pride: leaving our proper place and grasping the power to decide who is right and who is wrong, needing to win at all costs. Humility returns to our proper place and leaves judgment to God. People matter more than issues—on the other side of the screen is a person with a soul, not an account to be defeated.
think: What two images do Proverbs 26:17 and 20 use to describe quarreling?
When I argue online, is it for the truth and the other person’s sake, or to win?
What principle for my online words could I set for myself?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that online I am often stirred up and meddle in quarrels not my own, wanting to win. Forgive my pride, and remind me that the person on the other side of the screen is someone you love. Give me wisdom to know when to speak and when to stop, so that my words bring peace instead of adding wood to the fire. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if you feel the urge to respond to something controversial online, pray first and wait until tomorrow to decide. If you have ever said too much to someone online, apologize to them privately today.
lessons.quick: Without more wood, a quarrel dies down—you don’t have to win every battle.
text: Like one who grabs a dog’s ears is one who passes by and meddles in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman who shoots torches, arrows, and death,
is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, “Am I not joking?”
For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.
As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.
The words of a whisperer are as dainty morsels, they go down into the innermost parts.

lessons.title: Before You Hit Send
lessons.hear:
Proverbs says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely” (Proverbs 10:19). In the digital age, a multitude of words has never been easier. One tap and a sentence lands on hundreds of phones; another tap and it is forwarded to even more. So the one second before we hit send has become the second that most requires wisdom. Today, let’s practice three questions.

First, is it true? Family group chats are full of forwarded “urgent alerts,” “health secrets,” and “major events happening somewhere,” often never verified. Proverbs says, “A simple man believes everything, but the prudent man carefully considers his ways” (Proverbs 14:15). The law also says, “You shall not spread a false report” (Exodus 23:1). Forwarding a false message may look well-intentioned, but it can cause panic, get people scammed, or even harm innocent people. If you aren’t sure, don’t send it.

Second, is it necessary? Some things are true but aren’t mine to make public. Things people told you in confidence, screenshots of others’ conversations, calling someone out by name in a group—even if the content is accurate, it damages trust. Third, is it kind? Without tone of voice or facial expression, an “OK” can read as cold, and a question mark can read as an accusation. So online we need to add more warmth than we would face to face.

These questions remind us that silence can also speak. In every group chat, someone posts a message and nobody responds; that person may be sitting in front of the screen feeling ignored. One sister posted a question in her new church’s group chat, and no one answered all day. Just as she was about to leave the group, a brother she had never met messaged her privately: “Welcome! Let me ask around for you.” She said that one sentence is why she stayed. Today, you can be the one who responds.
lessons.light: “The lips of the righteous feed many” (Proverbs 10:21)—online, the reach of these words is magnified. One message from me can nourish people or mislead them. Relying on the Holy Spirit with my heart, I pause for one second before I hit send and ask the Lord: Will these words bring you glory?
think: In Proverbs 10:19-21, what marks wise lips?
Have I ever forwarded an unverified message, or left someone in a group chat feeling ignored?
Whose often-ignored message will I respond to today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, before I hit send, remind me to pause: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? Forgive me for forwarding carelessly, criticizing casually, and ignoring people in group chats who needed a response. Use my fingers today to pass on truth and warmth. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a message in one of your group chats that no one has answered, and give the sender a sincere reply or a caring private message. Before forwarding any news, check its source.
lessons.quick: Three questions before you hit send: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind?
text: He is in the way of life who heeds correction, but he who forsakes reproof leads others astray.
He who hides hatred has lying lips. He who utters a slander is a fool.
In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.
The tongue of the righteous is like choice silver. The heart of the wicked is of little worth.
The lips of the righteous feed many, but the foolish die for lack of understanding.

lessons.title: No Time Even to Eat
lessons.hear:
The disciples had just returned from their mission and were excitedly reporting to Jesus everything they had done and taught. At that time “there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat” (Mark 6:31). It sounds a lot like modern life: one message after another, group chats that always have a red dot, answering work messages even during meals. It isn’t that we aren’t doing anything; we are doing too much, and we can’t stop.

Jesus said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile” (Mark 6:31). This was Jesus’ own invitation. He wasn’t scolding his disciples for not working hard enough; he was protecting them. People who are always giving will soon run dry unless they return to the source.

Let’s review ourselves honestly today: Can I get through a meal without looking at my phone? When I open my eyes in the morning, is the first thing I look to God or my notifications? When I sit at the table with my family, are we really together, or each lost in our own screen? When I reply to messages instantly, is it out of love, or out of fear of missing out or being seen as irresponsible?

Martha is a mirror for us. When Jesus came to her home, she was busy serving, her heart in a whirl, and she even complained to the Lord that her sister wasn’t helping. Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41-42). Martha’s busyness wasn’t wrong; what was wrong was letting busyness replace being with the Lord. Later, when Lazarus died, it was Martha who made a beautiful confession of faith in Jesus (see John 11:27). She wasn’t condemned; she was invited back to the one thing that is needed.

Adjustment can start small: no phones at the table during meals; a set time each day with notifications off; the last half hour before bed spent handing the day over to God. If you find you have been anxious for a long time and can’t put your phone down, you can also talk with someone you trust or a professional counselor—that too is God’s grace.
lessons.light: Behind our inability to stop there is often the self-centered life: fear of missing out, fear of being forgotten, the feeling that nothing can happen without me. Selfless people can set things down for a while, because they know the world is in God’s hands. Relationships have an order: God first. Only when we first go to a deserted place to be with the Lord can we return to people and truly love them.
think: In Mark 6:30-32, why did Jesus invite his disciples to “rest awhile”?
Behind my inability to stop checking my phone, what am I afraid of missing—or afraid of facing?
What small place can I start today to let my phone go quiet?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you invite me to come away to a deserted place with you and rest awhile. I confess that, like Martha, my heart is often in a whirl, chased by messages and notifications. Teach me to put my phone down and return to the one thing that is needed. Let me find rest in you, and be truly present with the people around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today at dinner, put your phone in another room and give your full attention to the family or roommates at the table. Ask at least one caring question, and listen to the whole answer.
lessons.quick: Those who are always giving must first return to the source and rest.
text: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

lessons.title: Digital Sabbath: Back to God and People
lessons.hear:
The longest of the Ten Commandments is the one about rest: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:8-10). Why did God write rest into his commandments? Because he knows that unless we are commanded to stop, we will hardly ever truly stop.

The Sabbath has two emphases. First, it remembers God: “for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11). To stop is to acknowledge that the world isn’t held up by me; God is in charge. Second, it is about relationships: on this day not only I, but my sons and daughters, my servants, even the foreigner living in my town are to rest (see Exodus 20:10). Sabbath isn’t a solo affair; it is a family, a community, returning together to God—and to one another.

Different traditions understand how to keep the Sabbath in different ways, but Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Rest is God’s gift to us. In the digital age, that gift can take a new form: a digital Sabbath—regularly setting aside a block of time to turn off notifications, put down our screens, give our hearts to God, and give our time to the real people around us. The app’s Digital Sabbath feature can help you schedule this time and remind you to read Scripture, pray, and be with your family during it.

These past few days we have learned to speak words that build up online, not to grab the dog’s ears, to pause a second before hitting send, and to come back to the Lord from our busyness. Today, let’s put all this into a rhythm and invite others to join us: agree with your family on a screen-free evening, agree with your small group to put phones in a basket during meetings, agree with a spiritual companion on a weekly digital Sabbath and check in with each other. When a group of people rests together, it becomes a new way of life that shows those around us: our hearts have one Lord, and we are not ruled by screens.
lessons.light: Sabbath lets God be God and lets us be human: we stop and acknowledge that God is in charge of the world. A digital Sabbath isn’t only abstaining; it is returning—first to our relationship with God, then to our relationships with people. A community that rests together lives out the rhythm of God’s system in everyday life.
think: In Exodus 20:8-11, what are the reason for the Sabbath and the scope of who rests?
These past few days, what progress have I made in my online words and in putting my phone down?
Whom will I invite to keep a regular digital Sabbath with me?
lessons.speak: God who made heaven and earth, thank you for giving me rest as a gift. I confess that I often act as if the world depends on me to hold it up. Help me regularly put down my screens and return to you, and to the real people beside me. Use me to invite my family and companions to enter your rest together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, use the app’s Digital Sabbath feature to schedule a screen-free block this week, and invite a family member or spiritual companion to join you—plan a meal or a walk together that day.
lessons.quick: Stop and acknowledge that God is in charge; put down the screen and return to real people.
text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
You shall labor six days, and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
