weeks.title: Healthy Boundaries
weeks.theme: A boundary isn’t a wall but a guard over the heart God has entrusted to us—even Jesus said “no.”
group: Read Mark 1:32-39. When “everyone is looking for you,” what choice did Jesus make?
Who do you find it hardest to say “no” to? What are you afraid of underneath?
How will you use healthy boundaries this week to love someone more genuinely?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, set aside some time alone and, with prayer, look over your calendar and your phone: Which commitments come from love, and which come from fear? Then choose someone you have long wanted to spend time with but who keeps getting crowded out, and invite them for tea or a walk, giving them your time for real. When you get home, thank God for both your limits and his abundance.

lessons.title: Keep Your Heart Above All
lessons.hear:
Speaking as a father to his son, Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). To “keep” here means to watch over and guard, like a watchman at a city gate or a hedge around an orchard. A city without gates lets anyone come and go; it looks open, but it will soon be plundered. A garden without a hedge looks generous, but in the end nothing grows there.

That is what a boundary is. Many Christians think love means always saying “yes,” always being on call, never letting anyone down—as if having boundaries means we don’t love enough or aren’t spiritual enough. But the biblical picture is just the opposite. A boundary isn’t a wall built to keep people out; it guards the heart God has entrusted to me so that it can keep pouring out life. A wall is for shutting out; a hedge is for protecting. A wall says, “Don’t come near me”; a hedge says, “There is something here I need to take good care of.”

This passage in Proverbs goes on to speak of the mouth, the eyes, and the feet: put away a perverse mouth, let your eyes look straight ahead, make the path of your feet level (see Proverbs 4:24-26). Boundaries aren’t only about saying no to others; they are also about saying no to ourselves: not saying the hurtful word, not looking at what pollutes the heart, not walking down the path that leads astray. Only someone who can say no to himself is able to say a genuine yes to others.

Why must we guard our hearts? Because the love, patience, and kindness in our relationships are springs that flow from the heart. If that spring is trampled at will and drained without limit, all that eventually flows out is exhaustion, resentment, and bitterness. Guarding the heart isn’t selfish; it is how we keep on loving for the long haul. We need to learn loving boundaries: neither building walls nor tearing down every hedge.
lessons.light: A self-centered boundary is a wall: it protects only my own comfort. Having no boundaries is often self-centered too: afraid of rejection, wanting to be needed. A selfless boundary is a guard: it keeps the heart God has entrusted to me, lets Jesus reign there, and lets lasting love flow out of it. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life, and the Holy Spirit lives in the heart.
think: In Proverbs 4:23-27, what are we told to guard?
Is my heart like a city without gates, a fortress behind high walls, or a garden with a hedge?
What is one thing today for which I need to say “no” or “yes” in order to guard my heart?
lessons.speak: Father, you have entrusted my heart to my keeping. I confess that sometimes I let anyone come and go until I am worn out, and other times I build high walls and keep people at arm’s length. Teach me to keep my heart with all diligence; give me hedges instead of walls, so that your life may flow from my heart to others for a long time to come. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list every commitment you have this week and circle one you agreed to out of fear. Also think of someone you truly want to spend quality time with, and message them today to set up a time to meet.
lessons.quick: A boundary isn’t a wall but a hedge: guard your heart so you can keep on loving.
text: My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings.
Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart.
For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body.
Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you.
Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you.
Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.
Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.

lessons.title: Even Jesus Said No
lessons.hear:
A sister who leads a small group kept her phone on twenty-four hours a day. When group members messaged her in the middle of the night to pour out their troubles, she always replied. When someone needed her to cover a shift at the last minute, help them move, or lend them money to get by, she never said no. She thought, “I’m the small group leader; I have to deny myself like Jesus.” Then one day she screamed at her kids at home and afterward cried alone in the bathroom: “I’m good to everyone except my own family—I have nothing left for them.”

Behind this lies an old mindset: love means never refusing; saying no is unspiritual. But look at Jesus. One evening, “All the city was gathered together at the door” (Mark 1:33), and Jesus healed many. The next day, “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The disciples found him and said, “Everyone is looking for you” (Mark 1:37). That sounds like the best ministry opportunity imaginable. But Jesus said, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason” (Mark 1:38).

Jesus said “no” to “everyone is looking for you.” Not because he didn’t love them, but because he was clear about the mission the Father had given him, and he had first drawn strength in the Father’s presence. His boundaries came from two things: his relationship with the Father and a clear calling. Self-denial is for Jesus and for others, not for feeding the feeling of being needed. If we say yes to everything, it is often not out of love but out of fear: fear of being thought badly of, fear of losing the relationship, fear of no longer being needed.

That sister eventually talked with her group: unless it was an emergency, messages after ten at night would be answered the next day. When it came to lending money, she honestly explained her principles and instead helped people connect with the church’s care ministry or other formal sources of help. She expected everyone to be disappointed, but one member said, “Actually, this makes me feel better too—I don’t have to worry about bothering you.” Boundaries didn’t make her love smaller; they made it go farther.
lessons.light: Never saying no often means “being needed” reigns, not Jesus. Jesus’ boundaries came from first being connected to the Father—this is the order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with people, then with tasks. When we are clear about our proper place and calling, we can say “yes” in love and also say “no” in love.
think: In Mark 1:35-38, what did Jesus do before he said “no”?
How much of my saying yes to others comes from love, and how much from fear?
Which request do I need to respond to in a gentle but clear way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when everyone was looking for you, you first went to a deserted place to pray and then obeyed the Father’s will by going elsewhere. Help me also to connect with you first and be clear about the calling you have given me. Forgive me for saying yes to everything in order to be needed, and give me courage to say “yes” in love and “no” in love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a request you have been reluctantly agreeing to and that has left you running on empty. Today, pray first, then gently and clearly explain to the person what you can and cannot do.
lessons.quick: Even Jesus said “no,” because he first said “yes” to the Father.
text: At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those who were possessed by demons.
All the city was gathered together at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. He didn’t allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Simon and those who were with him searched for him.
They found him and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason.”
He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons.

lessons.title: Let Your Yes Be Yes
lessons.hear:
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one” (Matthew 5:37). People in his day were in the habit of swearing oaths—by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem—as if their words weren’t believable without an oath attached. Jesus said that his disciples’ words should be trustworthy in themselves: “yes” really means yes, and “no” really means no.

This is very practical teaching on boundaries. We often hover vaguely between yes and no. We say, “Sure, let’s see,” when we really don’t want to go; we say, “I’ll try my best,” when we already know we can’t do it; to avoid offending someone we pile up excuses or even tell little white lies. The other person ends up waiting in vain, we end up feeling guilty, and the relationship gets worse. A vague “yes” often hurts more than a clear “no.”

Today, practice speaking clearly. First, pause instead of agreeing right away. You can say, “Let me think about it and get back to you tomorrow.” That gives you room to pray and ask the Lord, “Is this what you want me to do?” Second, when you say “yes,” do it wholeheartedly—don’t agree and then complain and drag your feet. Third, when you say “no,” be gentle and clear without over-explaining. For example: “Thank you for thinking of me. I can’t this time, but I’d be glad to pray for you.” A gentle “no” can still carry love.

A young brother fresh into the workforce was often invited by coworkers to go drinking and singing karaoke late into the night. Every time, he said, “Sure, next time,” but he never once went, and his coworkers began to feel he wasn’t sincere. Eventually he told them honestly, “I don’t really go out drinking at night, but I’d love to go hiking or get brunch with you guys on the weekend.” Two coworkers actually went with him. A clear boundary opened a door to genuine friendship.
lessons.light: A vague “yes” is often self-centered: afraid of offending people, wanting to protect our image. A clear “yes” or “no” is selfless honesty—not for saving face, but for real relationships. The Bible is my standard: speaking simply and honestly is how we let Jesus reign over our commitments.
think: In Matthew 5:33-37, why does Jesus say we don’t need to swear oaths?
With which kinds of requests do I most often give a vague “yes”?
Which request will I answer today with a clear “yes” or “no”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your yes is always yes; you are never vague. Forgive me for so often giving vague agreement to save face, leaving others waiting and myself feeling guilty. Give me an honest and gentle tongue, so that when I say “yes” I do it wholeheartedly, and when I say “no” I still say it with love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, respond to an invitation or request you have been putting off. If you should accept, say yes clearly and set a time; if you should decline, explain gently and offer another way you can show care.
lessons.quick: A vague “yes” often hurts more than a clear “no.”
text: “Again you have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not make false vows, but shall perform to the Lord your vows,’
but I tell you, don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God;
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shall you swear by your head, for you can’t make one hair white or black.
But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

lessons.title: Jethro: This Is Not Good
lessons.hear:
After Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt, he sat every day judging the people’s cases, and the people stood around him from morning till evening (see Exodus 18:13). His father-in-law Jethro saw this and said something very direct: “The thing that you do is not good. You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone” (Exodus 18:17-18).

Moses wasn’t lazy or selfish; he was too conscientious, too responsible. He probably thought, “The people need me. I can’t push this off on anyone.” But Jethro saw another reality: when one person carries everything, not only does he collapse, but the people suffer too. Jethro proposed a correction: Moses would keep doing what only he could do—standing before God for the people and teaching them God’s statutes—while choosing men who feared God and were trustworthy to share the work: “every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you” (Exodus 18:22).

This picture explains two of Paul’s statements that seem to contradict each other: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), and “each man will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5). Some burdens are too heavy and need the community to share them; yet each person also has a portion that is theirs to carry, which they shouldn’t push onto others, and which others shouldn’t take over completely. Healthy boundaries mean sorting out what is mine, what is theirs, and what we need to carry together.

Let’s examine ourselves: Like Moses, am I carrying burdens at home, at church, or at work that don’t belong to me? Is it because of love—or because I don’t trust others, can’t let go, or even believe that “nothing works without me”? The beauty of Moses is that he listened to his father-in-law and did what he said. Humbly accepting counsel and being willing to let go is where adjustment begins.
lessons.light: “Nothing works without me” is hidden pride: leaving our proper place as human beings and grasping a burden only God can bear. Humility lays down power, returns to our proper place, and gives others the chance to serve too. This is the spirit of 235—not one lone hero, but comrades-in-arms in a five-fold ministry team carrying the load together.
think: In Exodus 18:17-23, how did Jethro redistribute Moses’ load?
What burdens am I carrying right now that aren’t really mine, or that I shouldn’t carry alone?
Whom can I invite to share the load? And which portion is mine to carry faithfully?
lessons.speak: Father, like Moses I often think I have to carry everything myself, until I am exhausted and the people around me suffer too. Forgive the pride in my heart that says, “Nothing works without me.” Give me a humble heart to accept counsel, to learn to let go and trust others, and to faithfully carry the portion you have given me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify one thing you have been carrying alone and invite a family member, ministry team member, or coworker to share it. Explain specifically what you need help with, and thank them sincerely.
lessons.quick: Bear one another’s burdens—and let each carry his own load.
text: Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”

lessons.title: Safety First: I Can’t Come Down
lessons.hear:
Nehemiah was leading the people in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, and the work was nearly finished. His enemies sent an invitation: “Come! Let’s meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono” (Nehemiah 6:2). It sounded like peace talks, but Scripture cuts straight to the point: “But they intended to harm me” (Nehemiah 6:2). Nehemiah’s answer was clear: “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down” (Nehemiah 6:3). Four times they sent the same invitation, and each time he gave the same answer (see Nehemiah 6:4).

Some boundaries are not only for guarding the heart but for guarding our safety. Loving people doesn’t mean putting ourselves in danger; forgiving doesn’t mean allowing someone to keep hurting us; gentleness doesn’t mean accepting manipulation and threats without question. When people were plotting to kill Paul, his disciples “let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket” (Acts 9:25). Proverbs says, “A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3).

Today, this might look like: someone you met online who keeps pressing to meet you alone or asking you to send money; an ex who repeatedly follows you, checks up on you, or threatens you; verbal or physical harassment at work; a child being bullied at school or online; an older relative getting a phone call from someone claiming to be family in urgent need of money. In situations like these, safety comes first. You don’t need to stay silent to save face or to avoid “making a big deal of it.” You can block the person, keep evidence, tell someone you trust, and when necessary call the police or seek professional help. This isn’t a lack of love; it is wisdom, and it honors the life God has given.

Today, pass this wisdom on. There may be a friend, an older person, or a young person near you who is stuck in an unhealthy or even dangerous relationship and doesn’t know they can say no. You can gently come alongside them and tell them, “This isn’t your fault. You deserve to be respected. I’ll go with you to get help.” Sometimes the church’s most beautiful love is standing beside someone as they bravely say “no.”
lessons.light: The purpose of boundaries is to protect the life God has entrusted to us—not to build walls, and not to let ourselves be trampled. Jesus laid down his life for us, yet when his time had not yet come, he passed right through the middle of those who wanted to harm him (see Luke 4:30). Discerning when to deny ourselves and when to protect ourselves takes relying on the Holy Spirit with our hearts; walking with someone who is trapped toward safety is how love multiplies.
think: In Nehemiah 6:1-4, how did Nehemiah see through that invitation and respond to it?
Are there boundaries I need to set in my life for the sake of safety?
Who around me might be trapped in a dangerous relationship? How can I help them seek help?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for treasuring my life and the life of everyone who is being harmed. Give me discernment like Nehemiah’s to see through manipulation and danger and to bravely say “no.” And use me to gently walk alongside those around me who are trapped, toward safety and healing. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, reach out to a friend or older person you are concerned about and remind them to watch out for online scams and unhealthy relationships. If they are being threatened, help them contact someone they trust or the appropriate authorities.
lessons.quick: Love doesn’t mean walking into danger; when needed, say “no” and help others reach safety.
text: Now when it was reported to Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and to the rest of our enemies that I had built the wall, and that there was no breach left in it (though even to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates),
Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, “Come! Let’s meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono.” But they intended to harm me.
I sent messengers to them, saying, “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down. Why should the work cease while I leave it and come down to you?”
They sent to me four times like this; and I answered them the same way.

weeks.keyText: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

weeks.title: Loneliness and Solitude
weeks.theme: Loneliness locks us in a cave; solitude brings us to God—and then sends us back to people.
group: Read 1 Kings 19:1-18. Step by step, how does God care for Elijah and restore him?
Do you more often experience loneliness or intentional solitude? How are the two different in your life?
Which lonely person are you willing to keep company with this week, and what is one concrete way you will love your neighbor?
weeks.sunday: First give yourself thirty minutes of solitude. Go to a park or sit by a window, slowly read Psalm 142, and tell God honestly what is in your heart. Then carry that peace with you to visit an elderly person who lives alone or a neighbor who has just moved in. Bring a simple snack and chat with them about how life has been. Pray for them before you head out; when you get home, give thanks for the encounter and write down one prayer request they mentioned.

lessons.title: The Wilderness Before Dawn
lessons.hear:
It had been an exhausting day. “At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those who were possessed by demons. All the city was gathered together at the door” (Mark 1:32-33). Jesus healed the sick and cast out demons late into the night. If it had been us, we would probably have thought the next morning, “Strike while the iron is hot—the crowds are here!” But Mark records a quiet scene instead: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35).

Let’s pull apart two words we often blur together: loneliness and solitude. Loneliness is being disconnected. There may be people all around you, yet no one who truly understands you; your group chats are buzzing, but late at night you can’t think of a single name you could call. Solitude, on the other hand, is a choice: stepping away from people for a while in order to meet with God. Loneliness is like a house during a blackout—everything is dark. Solitude is like turning off a noisy TV and finally hearing your family talking to you.

Jesus’ solitude was not an escape. When the disciples tracked him down and said, “Everyone is looking for you” (Mark 1:37), he did not let the crowd’s demands pull him along. Instead he said they would go on to the nearby towns to preach. In the wilderness he had reconfirmed his direction with the Father. Solitude kept him from being swallowed by the crowd, yet it never made him abandon the crowd—his very next step was into more villages.

So this is the route for our week: from loneliness to solitude, and from solitude back to people. If you feel lonely right now, God isn’t asking you to get strong first and then come to him. He invites you to bring your loneliness into his presence, so that the empty room where “there’s no one” becomes a wilderness where you meet him. There you will discover that you are known and loved. And then you will find the strength to turn around and know and love another lonely person.
lessons.light: The root of loneliness is often that the order of our relationships has broken down. Solitude restores our relationship with God first, and then brings us back into right relationship with ourselves and with others. Jesus is my example: he went to the Father before dawn, so he did not lose his way in the crowds. Our focus is on Jesus—not on the applause of the crowd, and not on our own emptiness.
think: In Mark 1:32-39, what happened before and after Jesus’ time alone?
Is my recent loneliness about being cut off from people, or about lacking time alone with God?
Which ten minutes tomorrow morning can I set aside to come quietly before God?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, even at your busiest you went into the wilderness to meet with the Father. I confess that I am often afraid of quiet, and I fill my loneliness by scrolling on my phone. Please turn my loneliness into time alone with you. Let me rediscover your love there, and give me strength to walk back toward people and love those you have placed beside me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, leave your phone outside your bedroom. Tomorrow when you wake up, don’t check messages first—spend ten minutes reading Mark 1:35-39, and pray for someone you know has been lonely lately.
lessons.quick: Loneliness is being cut off; solitude is meeting with God.
text: At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those who were possessed by demons.
All the city was gathered together at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. He didn’t allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Simon and those who were with him searched for him.
They found him and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason.”
He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons.

lessons.title: The Meal Under the Juniper Tree
lessons.hear:
A brother in his early thirties moved alone to another city for work. By day he was busy at the office; by night he came home to a small rented studio where his only companions were takeout containers and the glow of his phone. On weekends he didn’t really want to go to church either, because the moment he walked in someone would ask, “How have you been?” and he didn’t know what to say. A voice inside kept telling him, “If you’re this lonely, something must be wrong with your faith.”

That is an old mindset many of us carry: loneliness means I’m not spiritual enough. But look at Elijah. He had just seen God send fire on Mount Carmel, yet in no time a single threat from Jezebel sent him running for his life. He went alone into the wilderness, sat down under a juniper tree, and asked to die: “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4). This was a great prophet, not a man of little faith. His loneliness and despair were the result of body, mind, and spirit all running dry at once.

How did God respond? No rebuke, no sermon. An angel touched him and said, “Arise and eat!” (1 Kings 19:5). He ate, then slept again. The angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). God cared for his body first—letting him eat and sleep—and only later spoke with him at Horeb. This is God’s perspective: you are a whole person. Your exhaustion, your sleepless nights, your lost appetite—he sees all of it, and he cares about all of it.

So if loneliness or depression has been weighing on you for a long time, affecting your sleep, appetite, and work, please don’t simply blame yourself for not praying enough. Seeking counseling or medical help is also God’s grace, just like that jar of water and that cake baked on the coals. Eventually that brother found the courage to tell his small group leader. The leader went with him to see a doctor and started inviting him to dinner every week. He said, “I thought God was far away from me. Actually, he sent someone to tap me on the shoulder.”
lessons.light: Self-centered loneliness often says, “It must be because I’m not good enough.” Being selfless doesn’t mean denying weakness; it means admitting that I am a creature who needs to eat, needs to sleep, and needs people. Returning to my proper place as a human being means letting God care for the whole of me. Letting people be people includes allowing myself to receive help.
think: In what order did God care for Elijah? Why food and sleep first?
Do I blame all of my loneliness or low moods on not being “spiritual enough”?
What care does my body need this week? Whom am I willing to tell how I’m really doing?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for treating me as you treated Elijah—not rebuking me first, but caring for me first. I confess that sometimes I am very tired and very lonely, yet I don’t dare say so. Make me willing to receive the help you give through people and through healing, and make me that jar of water and that cake under someone else’s juniper tree. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite a friend or small group member who has been showing up less often to share a meal, or drop off a meal at their home. Don’t rush to ask spiritual questions—just keep them company and enjoy a good meal together.
lessons.quick: God let Elijah eat and sleep before he ever spoke to him.
text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
When he saw that, he arose and ran for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
The LORD’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.

lessons.title: Pouring Out in the Cave, Reaching Out to Others
lessons.hear:
The heading of this psalm tells us it is David’s prayer from the cave. Hunted by Saul and hiding in a cave, David spoke words many people can’t bring themselves to say late at night: “Look on my right, and see; for there is no one who is concerned for me. Refuge has fled from me. No one cares for my soul” (Psalm 142:4).

Notice the first thing David did: he didn’t pretend. “I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles” (Psalm 142:2). Loneliness does its worst damage when it’s bottled up. Bottled-up loneliness is like a sealed can that goes sour the longer it sits; pouring it out to God is like popping the lid and letting the light in. You can pray in the plainest words: “Lord, I’m so lonely today. No one even asked how I was.” God won’t think you’re not spiritual enough.

Then David’s gaze shifted: “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 142:5). At his loneliest moment in the cave, he took hold again of the deepest relationship of all. The psalm ends with hope: “The righteous will surround me” (Psalm 142:7). And historically, it was in the cave of Adullam that a band of people in distress and discontent gathered around David one after another (see 1 Samuel 22:1-2). Very often, God answers loneliness by sending a person.

Today’s practice has two steps. First, pour it out to God: write down or speak your real feelings, with no polish. Second, reach out to others: think about who around you might also be in a “cave”—an elderly person living alone, an international student newly arrived overseas, the one in your group chat who hasn’t said anything in ages, a coworker who just lost their job. You don’t need to say much. One sincere greeting is a way of “looking on their right” for them. You may be lonely yourself, but when you reach out a hand to steady someone else, you will often find your own hand being held.
lessons.light: In 920, the “2” stands for every person connected to me—including the one who is about to be forgotten. Self-centered loneliness only sees that “no one cares for my soul”; selfless love turns and asks, “Who else has no one who cares?” When we let Jesus reign, he turns me from a victim in the cave into the righteous one standing beside someone else.
think: In Psalm 142, how does David’s gaze move from his circumstances to God?
Have I kept my loneliness bottled up, not even daring to tell God?
Who around me might be in a “cave” right now? How will I reach out to them today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I pour out my loneliness honestly before you; you know my way. You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living. Open my eyes to see those around me who are lonely too, and give me courage to reach out first and be the one you send. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, text or call someone who lives alone or has just moved somewhere new, and ask specifically: “Is there a day this week we could grab a meal or go for a walk together?”
lessons.quick: Pour out your loneliness to God, then reach out to the lonely.
text: I cry with my voice to the LORD. With my voice, I ask the LORD for mercy.
I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles.
When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, you knew my route. On the path in which I walk, they have hidden a snare for me.
Look on my right, and see; for there is no one who is concerned for me. Refuge has fled from me. No one cares for my soul.
I cried to you, LORD. I said, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.”
Listen to my cry, for I am in desperate need. Deliver me from my persecutors, for they are too strong for me.
Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will surround me, for you will be good to me.

lessons.title: You Are Not the Only One Left
lessons.hear:
In a cave on Mount Horeb, God asked Elijah the same question twice: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). Both times Elijah gave the exact same answer, ending with: “I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away” (1 Kings 19:10).

Those words carry real pain—and a bit of distortion. The pain is real: he truly was being hunted and isolated. The distortion is that when loneliness lasts long enough, we start using a single story to interpret everything: “I’m the only one who cares.” “No one understands me.” “Everyone leaves me.” Once that story hardens, it’s like putting on gray-tinted glasses—even other people’s kindness looks half-hearted. Often a bit of self-centeredness hides inside it: our focus narrows more and more onto ourselves, until our own grievances become the center of the world.

God didn’t argue with Elijah. Instead, he did three things. First, he revealed himself in a still, small voice, letting Elijah know he had been there all along. Second, he gave Elijah a new assignment so he wouldn’t stay stuck in the cave. Third, he corrected Elijah’s story: “Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel” (1 Kings 19:18), and he sent him to anoint Elisha as his companion and successor. God heals loneliness not only with comfort, but by bringing people back into community.

Today, examine yourself: Is there an “I’m the only one left” in my heart too? “No one at church cares about me.” “My coworkers are shutting me out.” Some of these are true; they need to be heard, and they’re worth talking through with someone you trust. Others are gray glasses that need correcting. The correction can be very concrete: write down three people who have shown you kindness this month, even if it was only a sticker or a quick hello. Then choose one and respond to them. You’ll discover that you are not the only one left.
lessons.light: Elijah’s “I, even I only, am left” is the voice of loneliness tangled up with self-centeredness. Our focus is on Jesus—not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When God turned Elijah’s eyes from the mouth of the cave to the seven thousand and to Elisha, he came back from fighting alone into God’s community. The spiritual companions of 235 are one of God’s gifts for healing loneliness.
think: How did God respond to Elijah’s claim that he alone was left?
Is there an “I’m the only one left” in my heart? How much of it is true, and how much is gray glasses?
Which person who has shown me kindness will I respond to this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you sought Elijah in a still, small voice, and you seek me too. I confess that I often say “No one understands me,” yet I fail to see the people you have long since placed beside me. Take off my gray glasses, correct the story in my heart, and bring me out of the cave and back into your community. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three people who have shown you kindness this month. Choose one, send them a message of thanks, and set a time to meet up next.
lessons.quick: Long loneliness tells lies: you are not the only one left.
text: He came to a cave there, and camped there; and behold, the LORD’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

He said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD.” Behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake a fire passed; but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
The LORD said to him, “Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.
Anoint Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel; and anoint Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel Meholah to be prophet in your place.
He who escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and he who escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.
Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him.”

lessons.title: Yet I Am Not Alone
lessons.hear:
On the eve of his suffering, Jesus told his disciples ahead of time: “You will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

This is one of the loneliest situations in the whole Bible: his closest friends were about to run away, and he would walk to the cross alone. Yet Jesus said, “I am not alone.” His security did not come from how many people were around him, but from a relationship with the Father that had never been broken. This is exactly the truth we want to anchor this week: solitude roots us in God, so that even when the crowds scatter, loneliness will not swallow us.

What’s more, Jesus went even further for us. On the cross he personally experienced the pain of being forsaken (see Mark 15:34), so that those who believe in him would never be abandoned by God. That is why we can declare that he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). He has tasted your loneliness; he has walked through your long nights.

This week we set out from the wilderness before dawn, passed by Elijah’s juniper tree, David’s cave, and the still, small voice on Horeb, and have finally arrived at these words of Jesus. Please pass this route on: loneliness is being cut off; solitude is meeting with God; and those who meet with God will walk back toward people. Today, share it with one person—maybe your small group, maybe a lonely friend. You don’t need to preach. Just say, “This week I learned that when I’m lonely, I can go to God first, and then God helps us find each other. Want to try it together?” Your sharing may be the very hand God sends to tap someone on the shoulder.
lessons.light: Repetition turns “I am not alone” from head knowledge into heartfelt conviction; multiplication lets another lonely person hear these words too. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head: the Holy Spirit lives in us, and he is the Counselor who is with us forever.
think: In John 16:32, why could Jesus say, “I am not alone”?
This week, as I moved from loneliness toward solitude, what small change took place in me?
With whom will I share what I received this week, and how?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, in your loneliest hour you still said, “I am not alone,” and you bore the pain of being forsaken for me so that I would never be abandoned. Let this assurance take root in my heart, and make me someone who passes on your presence, so that another lonely person may know: you are here, and so are we. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send John 16:32 to a friend who is lonely or facing hardship, add a few words of your own, and invite them to go for a walk or have a cup of tea with you this weekend.
lessons.quick: Whoever is with the Father is never alone, even when the crowd scatters.
text: His disciples said to him, “Behold, now you are speaking plainly, and using no figures of speech.
Now we know that you know all things, and don’t need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came from God.”
Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?
Behold, the time is coming, yes, and has now come, that you will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.
I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”

weeks.keyText: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.

weeks.title: Forgiveness: Setting Others and Ourselves Free
weeks.theme: Forgiveness doesn’t deny the hurt; it tears up the IOU, hands judgment to God, and walks out of the prison of bitterness.
group: Read Matthew 18:21-35. What does the contrast between “ten thousand talents” and “one hundred denarii” help you see?
Have you ever thought forgiveness meant pretending nothing happened and making up right away? How has your view changed this week?
Which person who has hurt you are you willing to bless in prayer this week, or for whom will you do a small act of neighborly love?
weeks.sunday: Find a quiet time to slowly read the Lord’s Prayer together with your spouse, family, or a trusted companion. Each of you silently hands one “IOU” over to God—there’s no need to share details. Afterward, share a simple meal and bless one another. If anyone is still in an ongoing harmful situation, talk together about how to protect their safety first and whom to ask for help. Finish by giving thanks that God has forgiven our ten thousand talents.

lessons.title: Ten Thousand Talents and a Hundred Denarii
lessons.hear:
Peter thought he was being very generous: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). For someone who has been wronged, seven times is already a lot of patience. But Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). He didn’t mean you should count to four hundred ninety. He meant: stop counting.

Then Jesus told a parable. A servant owed the king ten thousand talents—an astronomical sum he could never repay in one lifetime, or ten. The king was moved with compassion and canceled all of it. Yet as soon as that servant walked out, he ran into a fellow servant who owed him one hundred denarii, grabbed him by the throat, and had him thrown into prison. The point of the parable is proportion: what we owed God is ten thousand talents; what others owe us, however painful, is a hundred denarii. That doesn’t mean your wound doesn’t matter. A hundred denarii is a real debt, and Jesus never said it was zero. But when I stand before the cross and see how much I have been forgiven, I find the strength to forgive others.

So what is forgiveness? Put simply, it is tearing up the IOU. I no longer demand that the other person pay me back with their own hands; I hand judgment and justice over to God. Notice that at the end of the parable, the one handed over to the tormentors is the servant who refused to forgive. Unforgiving people often think they have locked the other person up, but they are the ones serving the sentence—their chest tightens every time they remember what happened, and seeing that name pop up in a group chat ruins their whole day.

So this week’s theme is forgiveness: setting others free, and setting ourselves free. Jesus said we must forgive “from your hearts” (Matthew 18:35). That is usually not a single teeth-gritting decision but a process. Today, begin by asking the Holy Spirit to show you the grace of those ten thousand talents. Within that grace, you will find that the hundred-denarii IOU in your hand can slowly be set down.
lessons.light: A self-centered heart clings to the IOU, because “justice” seems safe only if I hold it in my own hand. A selfless heart knows it has been forgiven ten thousand talents, and so it returns to its proper place: I am a sinner saved by grace, not the final judge. Letting Jesus reign also means letting him deal with the debts I can never collect.
think: Why did the servant who had been forgiven a huge debt refuse to forgive a small one?
Is there a “hundred-denarii IOU” in my hand that I have refused to let go of?
How can I meditate today on the ten thousand talents I have been forgiven?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I owed you ten thousand talents, and in Christ you forgave it all. I confess that I often grab others by the throat over a hundred denarii, and bitterness has locked me in prison too. Show me how great your grace is, so that I can forgive from my heart, hand judgment over to you, and let both of us go free. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes writing down three things God has forgiven in your life. Then pray a simple sentence of blessing for someone you still have a knot in your heart about.
lessons.quick: Only those forgiven ten thousand talents find strength to forgive a hundred denarii.
text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.
But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’
The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt.
“But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’
“So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’
He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due.
So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

lessons.title: Am I in the Place of God?
lessons.hear:
Years ago, a sister lent a sum of money to a close friend from college. The friend later cut off contact and even told mutual friends that she was stingy and petty. Over the years she heard “You must forgive” many times at church, and each time it hurt more, because she thought forgiveness meant pretending nothing had happened, saying “It’s fine,” adding the friend back on social media, and hugging her with a smile at the next reunion. She couldn’t do it, so another layer of guilt piled onto her heart.

This is a common old mindset: forgiveness means denying the hurt and then reconciling immediately. Look at Joseph. His brothers sold him as a slave, and he was later thrown into prison for a crime he didn’t commit. After their father died, the brothers feared he would take revenge. Joseph did not say, “Oh, it’s nothing.” He stated the truth plainly: “As for you, you meant evil against me” (Genesis 50:20). Forgiveness doesn’t call evil good. It begins by honestly admitting: that was real harm.

Then Joseph said something weighty: “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). This is the heart of forgiveness: the judge’s seat belongs to God, not to me. Revenge is leaving our proper place and grasping power—God’s power; forgiveness gives that seat back to him. Then Joseph saw the bigger picture: “but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). God did not let evil have the last word.

Notice too that Joseph’s relationship with his brothers was not restored overnight. In Egypt he tested them again and again, and only revealed himself after he saw Judah willing to become a slave in Benjamin’s place (see Genesis 44:33-34). Forgiveness can be a one-sided, immediate decision made before God; trust, however, needs time and changed behavior to rebuild, and reconciliation takes two. That sister could lay down revenge before God and stop striking back behind her friend’s back. As for whether to lend money again or restore closeness, she could decide slowly and wisely. After praying that day she said, “So I can forgive without having to pretend.”
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power; revenge is wanting to sit in the judge’s seat. Joseph’s question, “Am I in the place of God?” is humility returning to its proper place: letting God be God and people be people. From a human perspective, it’s “He harmed me.” From God’s perspective, it’s “God meant it for good.”
think: How did Joseph both acknowledge the harm and hand judgment over to God?
Have I mistaken forgiveness for “pretending nothing happened” or “trusting again right away”?
Toward the person who hurt me, which part can I lay down before God today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you know that what happened truly hurt me, and I don’t have to pretend. Today I say with Joseph: Am I in your place? I give the judge’s seat back to you; please handle the justice I cannot handle. And give me wisdom to know how trust should be rebuilt step by step, or how to keep healthy boundaries. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: In prayer today, hand over to God the name of someone who hurt you, along with what they did, and say, “Judgment belongs to you.” Decide that this week you will not run that person down in front of anyone.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness doesn’t pretend; it gives the judge’s seat back to God.
text: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.title: Handing the IOU to the Father
lessons.hear:
Jesus taught us to pray every day: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). This line sits between “our daily bread” and “bring us not into temptation,” as if to remind us that forgiveness isn’t an occasional major event but as ordinary and daily as eating.

Why did Jesus put “being forgiven” and “forgiving others” together? Because they are like two ends of the same pipe. God’s grace flows in at one end, but if the other end is clogged with bitterness, the water can’t flow. After the prayer, Jesus added: “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). This is not a transaction; it reveals a spiritual reality. A hand clenched tightly around someone else’s IOU has a hard time opening to receive grace.

Today, put this into practice in a concrete way. Take a sheet of paper and write down a name that hurts every time you think of it. Then write down the “debt” they owe you: an insult, a betrayal, money never repaid, mockery in a group chat for everyone to see. Be specific, because forgiveness begins with honesty. Then slowly pray the Lord’s Prayer, pausing at “forgive us our debts,” and tell the Father: “I hand this IOU to you. I will no longer try to collect it myself, and I will no longer judge them over and over in my heart.” Finally, write on the paper: “Handed to God.”

Doing this won’t necessarily make the emotions vanish right away. They may come back tomorrow—then pray again. That is what “seventy times seven” looks like. There is also no need to rush to contact the other person; forgiveness happens first between you and God. If the person is still hurting you, please protect your own safety first and, when needed, seek help from someone you trust or from professionals. In that kind of situation, forgiveness never means staying in harm’s way.
lessons.light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Relying on our heads, we keep recalculating how much the other person owes; relying on the Spirit, we bring the IOU to the Father. The Lord’s Prayer first asks, “Let your Kingdom come,” and then, “Forgive us our debts”: wherever Jesus reigns, bitterness loses its ground.
think: In the Lord’s Prayer, which petitions surround “Forgive us our debts”? What does that suggest?
Which item on that IOU is hardest for me to let go?
Which specific person will I pray for today using the Lord’s Prayer?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, you have forgiven my debts—far more than I can count. Today I hand this IOU to you. I will no longer try to collect it myself or judge them over and over in my heart. When the feelings return, Holy Spirit, remind me to hand it over again, until I can sincerely bless them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, take ten minutes to write an IOU as described today. After praying the Lord’s Prayer, write “Handed to God” on it. Put the paper away and look at it again next week.
lessons.quick: Every time you pray “forgive us our debts,” hand one IOU to the Father.
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

lessons.title: A Heart Struck After Cutting the Robe
lessons.hear:
David had the perfect chance for revenge. Saul, who had hunted him for years, walked alone into the very cave where David was hiding. David’s men whispered excitedly: “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you’” (1 Samuel 24:4). Even God’s word was being used to justify revenge.

David didn’t kill Saul, but he quietly cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. Then the text says: “Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt” (1 Samuel 24:5). This is a very fine piece of self-examination. He didn’t use his sword on Saul, but he did something small with a hint of humiliation in it—and his conscience would not let it go.

That is exactly what we need to review today. People today rarely take revenge with a sword, but we often cut off a “robe corner”: deliberately leaving someone on read or never liking their posts; “casually” bringing up their embarrassing moments in front of others; posting something that names no names but that everyone understands; quietly dropping them from the dinner invite list. These little knives are the self-centered heart saying, “I want them to hurt a little too.” David’s correction was to hand judgment back to God: “May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you” (1 Samuel 24:12).

There’s one more important detail. When Saul heard this, he wept and said many kind things. But the story ends: “Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold” (1 Samuel 24:22). David forgave, but he did not naively follow Saul back to the palace. Forgiveness doesn’t mean restoring trust immediately. When someone is still hurting you, keeping your distance, protecting your safety, and seeking help from trusted people—or even the police—do not violate forgiveness. Ask yourself today: Is there a “robe corner” in my hand? Lay it down, and ask the Lord for wisdom to know when you can draw near and when you should go up to the stronghold.
lessons.light: Self-centered revenge is often small and hidden, yet it wounds just as much—and binds us just as much. Being selfless doesn’t mean letting others walk all over you; it means not raising your own hand, and leaving vindication to God. Humility sparks humility: when David put down his sword, Saul softened for a time. But wisdom also reminds us that trust depends on the other person’s change, and safety always comes first.
think: Why was David’s “heart struck” after he cut off the corner of Saul’s robe?
Have I recently “cut a robe corner” by leaving someone on read, dropping hints, or giving the cold shoulder?
In a particular relationship, what do I need right now—to draw near, to wait, or to keep my distance?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you search my heart. I confess that even though I have not raised a sword, I often cut at others’ robes with cold shoulders, insinuations, and gossip. Forgive me. Help me no longer to raise my own hand, but to leave vindication to you. And give me wisdom and discernment, with the courage to keep boundaries when I need to protect myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, review your social media posts and group messages. If anything hints at or belittles someone, delete it. Decide that this week you will not strike back at that person with coldness or insinuation.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness lays down the knife, but it needn’t naively follow Saul back to the palace.
text: He came to the sheep pens by the way, where there was a cave; and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were staying in the innermost parts of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’” Then David arose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave and cried after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth, and showed respect.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to men’s words, saying, ‘Behold, David seeks to harm you’?

Behold, today your eyes have seen how the LORD had delivered you today into my hand in the cave. Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed.’

Moreover, my father, behold, yes, see the skirt of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the skirt of your robe and didn’t kill you, know and see that there is neither evil nor disobedience in my hand. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt for my life to take it.
May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you.

lessons.title: Passing On a Word of Forgiveness
lessons.hear:
On the cross Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Not long afterward, as stones rained down on him, the first martyr, Stephen, knelt and cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” (Acts 7:60). Stephen’s prayer was almost an echo of Jesus’ prayer. Forgiveness gets passed on.

Even more remarkable, Luke points out one particular person at the scene: “The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul” (Acts 7:58). This Saul later became the apostle Paul. We can’t know what Stephen’s words of forgiveness left in his heart, but this man who once was “consenting to his death” (Acts 8:1) later wrote to the church: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). A word of forgiveness spoken under a hail of stones was like a seed falling into the most unlikely soil.

This week we have seen that forgiveness does not deny the hurt; it hands judgment to God. It is not pretending nothing happened; it is tearing up the IOU. It is not restoring trust immediately; it is letting God lead the next step of the relationship. Forgiveness frees us from the prison of bitterness and lets grace flow through us to the next person.

Today, practice it again and pass it on. Repeat: pray the Lord’s Prayer once more, and at “forgive us our debts,” bless the person who came to mind this week. Multiply: at home, in your small group, or with one friend, share one thing you learned this week—maybe that “forgiveness doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened,” or the IOU you handed over to God. Your children and your small group members are watching how you handle hurt. Your forgiveness today may become their example tomorrow.
lessons.light: From Jesus to Stephen to Paul, forgiveness has passed from one generation to the next—that is multiplication. The “9” in 920 is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, and forgiveness is one of the clearest fruits of Christ’s life in us. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when people see us forgive, they don’t see how great we are, but how powerful the cross is.
think: How is Stephen’s prayer similar to Jesus’ prayer?
This week, what step forward did I take on the road of forgiveness?
Will I share what I received this week with my family, my small group, or a particular friend?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the cross you asked forgiveness for those who crucified you, and Stephen prayed the same way for those who stoned him. Put that same life in me, so that my forgiveness not only sets me free but also becomes a window through which others can see you. May you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a family member, small group member, or friend and take five minutes to share one new insight about forgiveness from this week. Then invite them to pray the Lord’s Prayer with you.
lessons.quick: Jesus’ forgiveness passed to Stephen—and it must pass on through me.
text: But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears, then rushed at him with one accord.
They threw him out of the city and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!”
He kneeled down and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep.
